title: Pentagon lists 4 killed in Iran war under "Overseas Operations Casualties"
summary: Four U.S. service members who were listed in a Pentagon casualties database as having died during the Iran war are now listed as "Overseas Operations Casualties."
story: The Pentagon website that informs the public about the dead and wounded in military conflicts now lists four service members killed in Jordan and Iraq in July under "Overseas Operations Casualties" — separate from 14 other service members who have been killed during the war with Iran.

The other 14 appear in the database as casualties of Operation Epic Fury, the Defense Department's name for the conflict. At one point last week, the four service members' deaths also appeared on that list, but by last Thursday, their names no longer appeared there, and the database said that 14 were killed in the war with Iran, as opposed to 18.

The New York Times first reported the database's missing numbers and cited three sources who said it was because the four service members who were most recently killed died after the Trump administration had declared a ceasefire in April.

But the four service members were killed about a week after President Trump notified Congress by letter that the ceasefire was over and military action had resumed on July 7. The four who died are 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad, Pvt. Isabella Gonzales and Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton.

Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, in a statement shared on X last Thursday, blamed "site errors on the Defense Casualty Analysis System" on "a temporary data disruption" and said the "site anomalies are currently being resolved in coordination with the Military Services." Parnell in his statement slammed the New York Times for "colluding with anonymous sources to push a completely fake story."

When the Pentagon first released the names of two of the three killed in an Iranian attack in Jordan earlier this month, it initially classified them as deaths under Operation Inherent Resolve, the name for the years-long mission targeting ISIS. Later, the Defense Department amended the releases to say the service members had died in "overseas operations."

Throughout the war with Iran, the Pentagon has been slow to provide information about injuries. After the New York Times reported earlier this week that dozens of troops had been injured in attacks in the Middle East, the Pentagon initially referred reporters with questions on the wounded to the website — even though it had not been updated in several days and did not account for the recent deaths.
Defense officials have not briefed reporters on the Iran war since May, and they have not commented on the categorization of the deaths of the four service members.

CBS News first reported and Parnell confirmed that nearly 100 U.S. service members had been injured since July 7. In a statement on X, he said that among those injured, 96% had returned to duty and the vast majority of injuries experienced "were minor concussions." Minor concussions can often be traumatic brain injuries that vary in severity and can display symptoms some time after the initial injury.
He concluded by saying that "further updates will be posted on the Defense Casualty Analysis System."

As of Sunday, the site said 417 service members have been wounded in the war with Iran, which is dozens fewer than the 482 it listed early last week. Now, 207 service members are listed as having been wounded in Overseas Operations.

title: More than 300,000 displaced in France and Spain as wildfires rage
summary: Forests in Spain and France have been parched by successive heatwaves since May that have brought drought to many areas.
story: Fire crews in France and Spain continued to battle raging wildfires that have forced the evacuation of more than 300,000 people in the two countries.

Authorities in France's Gironde region, where the wine region city of Bordeaux is located, issued overnight evacuation orders for five more localities as shifting winds and arid conditions complicated the massive effort to limit the spread of the monster blaze. The evacuation operation now ranks among the biggest seen since World War II, authorities said, with more than 250,000 people ordered out of the danger zone in one region alone.
"The situation remains very unfavorable" for fires across France, the country's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez posted on X Sunday.

"The fire again became extremely virulent again and unpredictable, generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," Nunez posted on X. "It became calmer by the end of the night."

The area that has burned, much of it pine forests and scrubland made tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year, has grown inexorably, expanding by Sunday morning to an estimated 162 square miles, the Gironde prefecture said. That is seven times the area of Manhattan island and four times the size of Paris.

Firefighters are battling to slow the flames' progression toward Bordeaux, both on the ground and in the air, with planes dropping water and retardants. Soldiers have been called in to reinforce fire crews' exhausting round-the-clock efforts and other European countries have sent water-dropping planes, helicopters and firefighters.
Spanish firefighters engaging blaze on two fronts
Meanwhile in neighboring Spain, more villages in the fire zone raging west of Madrid were emptied overnight and a new front opened near the coastal city of Valencia.
"We still have some difficult hours ahead," Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Sunday, but the night was "very positive in terms of bringing the flames under control."
"The fire is beyond our capacity to extinguish," Juanfran Perez Llorca, Valencia's regional president, told reporters late Saturday, according to AFP.
Pilar Bernabe, the central government delegate to Valencia, wrote on X that "the night was very intense."
"Weather conditions are expected to deteriorate as the day progresses, so these hours are being used to battle the flames," she said.
In total, uncontrolled blazes in Spain this week have forced 116,000 people out of their homes.
Evacuees fretted about what they'll find when they're allowed to return.
"It looked like the apocalypse. You couldn't see anything. Everything was covered in ash," said Rocío Domínguez, who evacuated with her dog, Simba, from Chapinería, west of Madrid.
"We don't know when we get to the town, if we'll have half the house burned down or we'll have it intact or we won't have a house," she said. "All the clothes, all the memories, everything."

A wildfire in a bushy ravine in Manises, a suburb of Valencia, that raged out of control for four hours killed one man on Saturday, the local government said, marking Spain's first recorded death in the latest fires.

At the end of his Sunday Angelus prayer, Pope Leo XIV referenced "the devastating wildfires" in France and Spain and said: "I express my solidarity and invite everyone to pray for those affected and for the work of the rescue workers."
Tourists in Italy flee wildfire via boat
Hundreds of people in Italy were evacuated by sea as a wildfire swept through parts of the southern Adriatic coast, AFP reported.
"More than 400 tourists and beachgoers have been evacuated by sea, the only viable evacuation route," the coast guard said on its WhatsApp channel, adding that operations were ongoing.
Evacuees were being rescued from the area around the town of Peschici in the southern Puglia region. A coast guard spokesman told AFP that around 300 more people were expected to be evacuated.
"The situation is currently under control," Peschici Mayor Luigi d'Arenzo was quoted as saying by local daily Gazzetta del Mezzogiorno.

Last week, thousands of emergency workers battled scores of fires in Sicily and in the Calabria region, where a local official said arsonists had started fires by tying rags soaked in flammable liquid to the tails of stray cats to spread the flames.
One firefighter died after falling ill while battling the flames in Sicily, the interior minister said.

title: Suspect in Berlin LGBTQ+ parade attack has ties to Islamic "circles," police say
summary: Berlin police did not identify the suspect, who is still at large, by name but said that he was already known to police and is from Berlin.
story: Berlin police have identified a suspect with ties to Islamic "circles" in the German capital after a car plowed into a crowd at the city's LGBTQ+ parade Saturday, killing one person and injuring at least 16.
Berlin police spokesman Florian Nath told reporters that measures were underway against the suspect and that "our search for this person is proceeding at full speed."
He did not identify the suspect by name but said that he was already known to police and is from Berlin.
"Based on the investigators' initial findings, we have already identified a suspected perpetrator," Nath said. "He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin."
Police said some of the victims had life-threatening injuries. Firefighters and ambulances were out with many emergency staffers at the scene to attend to the victims.

In a post on X, police called on everyone to leave the premises of the event immediately. According to police, a car had driven into the Tiergarten park, near the route of the pride march, hitting several people. Police did not know how many officers had been deployed to the scene but that it was "definitely a lot of police."
Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner expressed shock, saying that "following a peaceful and vibrant pride parade, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner."
"This is an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society," Wegner said. "I have confidence in the police and security authorities, who will be working around the clock to investigate."
Hundreds of thousands of people had come to Berlin on Saturday to celebrate at Berlin's Pride parade, known in Germany as Christopher Street Day. It's one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ celebrations.

The Pride event in front of the city's iconic Brandenburg Gate in downtown was called off around 10:15 p.m. and a band's performance on stage was interrupted. People were urged to go home and to avoid taking the route through the Tiergarten park.
Before the incident, people had celebrated peacefully, marching through the city for hours, dancing to loud music, and cheering the around 80 floats that participated in the parade.

Julian Miethig, who had attended the LGBTQ+ party at the Brandenburg Gate earlier, said he had just wanted to go to an afterparty when he heard from a friend that "something bad happened there and there are a lot of fire trucks, a lot of emergency vehicles, ambulances."
He said he went to Tiergarten and was shocked that something like this could have happened at Berlin's pride celebrations.
"It's a dark day for the community," he said.

title: Pentagon website "anomalies" that removed names of 4 killed in Iran war remain
summary: The Pentagon website, which was last updated on July 22, still showed only 14 killed in the conflict as of Friday.
story: The Pentagon website that informs the public about the dead and wounded in different military conflicts removed four deaths from the war with Iran this week, showing that 14 service members have died, instead of the 18 who have been killed since the war began in February.

Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, in a statement shared on X on Thursday, said that "the site errors on the Defense Casualty Analysis System were due to a temporary data disruption" and the "site anomalies are currently being resolved in coordination with the Military Services."
The site, which was last updated on July 22, on Friday still showed only 14 killed in the conflict.

According to the Congressional Research Service, when an active-duty service member dies, the service "is required to complete a form (DD 1300 Report of Casualty) that includes circumstances related to death," and that information is then entered into the Defense Casualty database.

The New York Times first reported the database's missing numbers Thursday and cited three sources who said it was because the most recent four service members who were killed in Jordan and Iraq last week died after the Trump administration declared a ceasefire in April. But the four service members were killed about one week after President Trump notified Congress in a letter on July 10 that the ceasefire had ended and military action had resumed on July 7.
Deaths in the war with Iran have been listed on the website under Operation Epic Fury, the name the Pentagon gave to the war when it began in February.

When the Pentagon released the names of two of three killed in an Iranian attack in Jordan last week, it initially classified them as deaths under Operation Inherent Resolve, the name for the mission targeting ISIS. It later amended the releases to say the service members had died in "overseas operations."
Earlier this week, the four service members' deaths were listed under Operation Epic Fury. On Thursday, however, their names no longer appeared there.

There is another discrepancy, too. The "names of the fallen" under the operation only lists the names of 13 of the deceased service members, rather than 14. CBS News has reached out to the Navy, which has a "pending death" on the site in July. If confirmed, that would bring the death total to 14. There are no Navy service members currently listed among the names of the fallen under Epic Fury. The Navy identified Cmdr. Gabriel Edwards as missing following a helicopter's emergency landing in the Arabian Sea on July 1.
Parnell in his statement on X blamed the removals on data disruptions and site anomalies. He criticized the New York Times for "colluding with anonymous sources to push a completely fake story."

Throughout the war with Iran, the Pentagon has been slow to provide information about injuries. After the New York Times reported earlier this week that dozens of troops had been injured in attacks in the Middle East, the Pentagon initially referred reporters with questions on the wounded to the website — even though it had not been updated in several days and did not account for the recent deaths.
Defense officials have not briefed reporters on the Iran war since May.

CBS News first reported and Parnell confirmed that nearly 100 U.S. service members had been injured since July 7. In a statement on X, he said that among those injured, 96% had returned to duty and the vast majority of injuries experienced "were minor concussions." Minor concussions can often be traumatic brain injuries that vary in severity and can display symptoms some time after the initial injury.
He ended his statement by saying "further updates will be posted on the Defense Casualty Analysis System."

As of Friday, the site said 420 service members have been wounded in the war with Iran, which is dozens fewer than the 482 it listed earlier this week. A U.S. official told CBS News even that higher number would not accurately reflect the latest count of service members injured since the war began.

title: Monica Lewinsky's Lindsey Graham tribute draws criticism and praise for placing people over party: expert
summary: Experts say Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham after his death reflects her philosophy of people over party despite political disagreements.
story: Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham following his death sparked interest across the aisles, not only for her respectful candor, but also served as a reminder of the late senator's impact on history.
Lewinsky, 53, paid her respects to the late South Carolina senator shortly after his death earlier this month and gave followers insight on their decades-long connection.
Her non-partisan testimonial drew criticism online, but experts believed that her tribute was an authentic gesture which reflected her personal philosophy of people over party.
MONICA LEWINSKY RECALLS 'VERY DARK MOMENTS' AFTER SCANDAL, SURVIVING JUDGMENT BY 'BILLIONS OF STRANGERS'
Monica Lewinsky's tribute to late Senator Lindsey Graham drew criticism and praise. (Jamie McCarthy/WireImage/Getty Images)
Graham, who died July 11 after what his office described was a "brief and sudden illness," was one of the Republican Party's most influential voices with more than three decades of service.
His death prompted thousands of tributes, including one poignant message from the former White House intern.
MONICA LEWINSKY SAYS BILL CLINTON ‘ESCAPED A LOT MORE THAN I DID’ AFTER WHITE HOUSE SCANDAL

"I've disagreed with many (many) of Lindsey Graham’s choices and beliefs, but he was also — as one of the house managers on the '98 impeachment — the one who worked tirelessly to prove there was a smear campaign against me from inside the WH," Lewinsky posted on X shortly after his death.
When X users took umbrage with the homage, Lewinsky was quick to remind followers that her experience was "healing" after years of trauma from the Clinton scandal.
"Come on. He did not do it for you. The man was evil," one user wrote.
Lewinsky fired back, "I know he didn’t do it for me. i didn’t whitewash his history. but those actions were healing for me (and my family)… thanks for sharing your opinion."
SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS
Monica Lewinsky was 21 when she began an unpaid internship at the White House under the Clinton administration. (Getty Images)
Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Lewinsky's tribute "fits her clearly identified personal philosophy to a tee."

"She's not suddenly a Lindsey Graham fan — she's just honest enough to say he did one thing that mattered to her, and she's not going to let political disagreement erase that," Uthe said. "It works in her favor, and it's the kind of nuance that actually means something."
Uthe noted that Lewinsky's post was "nonchalant, direct, and completely unpolished in the best way."

"There's no performance to it — it reads like: 'Hey, he wasn't perfect, I disagreed with most of what he did, but he did this one thing for me and I appreciated it.' That's it. It's classy, and it's a stand-up thing to highlight in someone's death."
"She's not suddenly a Lindsey Graham fan — she's just honest enough to say he did one thing that mattered to her, and she's not going to let political disagreement erase that."

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.
Lindsey Graham was one of 13 house members who served in Clinton's impeachment trial. (David Hume Kennerly)
Graham argued during the hearings that former President Bill Clinton abused his powers. (Karin Cooper)

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

Graham was one of the 13 House members appointed to Clinton's impeachment trial, where he not only blasted the former president for lying under oath, but also argued to restore "honor and integrity to the office."

"You don’t even have to be convicted of a crime to lose your job in this constitutional republic if this body determines that your conduct as a public official is clearly out of bounds in your role," he said on the floor in January 1999.
"Impeachment is not about punishment. Impeachment is about cleansing the office. Impeachment is about restoring honor and integrity to the office."
"Impeachment is not about punishment. Impeachment is about cleansing the office. Impeachment is about restoring honor and integrity to the office."
The impeachment trial against the 42nd president began in January 1999 and ended Feb. 12. While Clinton was impeached by the house, he was acquitted of perjury and obstruction of justice charges.
Monica Lewinsky became a household name and was hounded in public following the affair. (Jeffrey Markowitz)

Holly Baird, crisis management expert and founder of Media Source PR, told Fox News Digital that Lewinsky's tribute made it clear that her appreciation for the late senator was limited to specific circumstances and "should not be interpreted as agreement with his broader political positions."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Lewinsky's advocacy has centered on fairness, empathy, and the lasting impact of public treatment," Baird said. "Acknowledging someone she disagreed with politically for treating her fairly is consistent with those broader themes and reflects the principles she has consistently emphasized throughout her public life."
She added, "The statement reflects the idea that personal gratitude and political disagreement can coexist."

"Acknowledging someone she disagreed with politically for treating her fairly is consistent with those broader themes and reflects the principles she has consistently emphasized throughout her public life."

Former White House spokesperson Alexandra LaManna, noted how Lewinsky has dedicated her life to "turning one of the most public personal humiliations in modern history into something that has helped countless other people feel seen."
Monica Lewinsky's mother, Marcia Lewis, testified before a grand jury about the presidential affair and alleged cover-up. (Larry Morris/The Washington Post)
Monica Lewinsky was honored earlier this year as the 2026 Woman of the 21st Century by the Women's Guild Cedars-Sinai. (ABImages)
"By speaking openly about her own experience, she has helped change the way we think about public shaming, power imbalances, and being defined by the worst moment of your life," LaManna said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So when she thanks Lindsey Graham for standing up for her at a time when almost no one else did, it doesn't read as politics – it reads as someone recognizing decency where she found it, even in a complicated story."
"By speaking openly about her own experience, she has helped change the way we think about public shaming, power imbalances, and being defined by the worst moment of your life."

Shortly after Graham's death, his sister, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., was appointed to temporarily fill her brother's seat. She later announced on Fox News that she would enter next month’s special primary election to run for a full term in the Senate.

title: White House fires back after John Mellencamp mocks Trump's Gulf of America during concert
summary: John Mellencamp paused his "Pink Houses" performance to mock Trump's Gulf of America executive order, prompting a sharp White House response.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
The White House is hitting back after John Mellencamp took direct shots at President Donald Trump's Gulf of America.
Mellencamp paused his Saturday night show Holmdel, N.J. to mock Trump's executive order to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" to "Gulf of America."
On Monday, Davis Ingle, WH Spokesman, shared a statement with Fox News Digital. "Nobody in their right mind cares what out-of-touch, woke Hollywood celebrities have to say," Ingle said.
John Mellencamp blasted President Donald Trump's Gulf of America name change during a recent show. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

"Nobody in their right mind cares what out-of-touch, woke Hollywood celebrities have to say."
While Mellencamp's band kept playing, the musician said sarcastically, "The Gulf of Mexico? Is that right? It’s not the Gulf of America? What a stupid f–----g idea."

President Donald Trump held a "Gulf of America" hat on the South Lawn of the White House in April 2025. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Brooks Nader suffered an accidental wardrobe malfunction after enjoying a beach day at the iconic Club 55 in Saint-Tropez. (Backgrid)

BROOKS NADER WOWS IN ICONIC RED ONE-PIECE BATHING SUIT AS 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT FILMS BEACH SCENES

title: Kelly Ripa's painful surgery leaves her unable to speak
summary: Mark Consuelos revealed Kelly Ripa's gum graft surgery left her unable to talk, sharing details of her painful recovery with guest Nick Jonas.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Kelly Ripa's painful dental surgery sidelined the daytime TV staple, forcing the famously chatty host into an unusual recovery that left husband Mark Consuelos revealing she couldn't even speak.
During Monday's show, Consuelos revealed Ripa had undergone gum graft surgery.
"Kelly sends her love," the "Live with Kelly and Mark" co-host told guest Nick Jonas. "Kelly had a little bit – well, it’s not a little – she had a gum graft surgery."
Gum graft surgery typically helps correct thinning or receding gums, according to Cleveland Clinic. Consuelos admitted Ripa had been recommended to have the surgery years ago.
CLAY AIKEN SAYS KELLY RIPA FEUD SPARKED THE 'MOST CATASTROPHIC' WEEK OF HIS LIFE
Kelly Ripa is recovering from a painful gum graft surgery that forced the daytime TV host to stop talking, according to husband Mark Consuelos. (Dia Dipasupil/WireImage)
"Her dentist said five years ago, ‘You can do it in about five years,’" Consuelos recalled. "And she joked, ‘I didn’t think I’d still be on the air in five years!’"
Consuelos revealed her lengthy recovery process includes not talking.
"Wow. That’s got to be the hardest thing she’s ever done," Jonas joked.
Describing Ripa as "such a great conversationalist," Consuelos hinted he might be having trouble getting the talk show host to follow doctor's orders.
"I’m trying to keep her to follow the rules, follow the directions," he said.
KELLY RIPA SAYS 'DESPERATE TIMES' LED HER TO GET COSMETIC PROCEDURE DONE ON HER BACKSIDE

Mark Consuelos revealed Kelly Ripa's unusually painful dental surgery has sidelined the "Live with Kelly and Mark" co-host, saying the recovery has been one of her toughest yet. (Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic)
As Ripa recovered at home, Consuelos said the toughest part wasn't the pain – it was convincing the famously curious TV host to stop checking on her healing gums and let the procedure do its work.

"Last night she was like, ‘Can you look?’ I’m like, ‘I’m not pulling your lip down,’" Consuelos said. Ripa instead got into position so Consuelos could check without touching her lip. "So I’m down there like, ‘It looks great!’"

Despite famously skipping novocaine at the dentist, Kelly Ripa admitted defeat after a painful gum graft surgery left her recovering at home and away from "Live with Kelly and Mark." (Lorenzo Bevilaqua/Disney via Getty Images)
The longtime actor said the surgery was especially alarming because Ripa rarely complains about pain, making this recovery stand out from any previous trip to the dentist.
"Yeah, it’s painful," he told Jonas. "But she famously doesn’t feel pain. When she goes into the dentist, she doesn’t use the novocaine. But this one hurts, so I know it’s bad."
Ripa's notoriously high pain tolerance led Jonas to marvel at just how much women can endure. He revealed his own wife, Danielle Jonas, has a similar ability to brush off pain.

title: 'You're So Vain' singer Carly Simon says Parkinson's and cancer diagnoses kept her from public eye
summary: "You're So Vain" singer Carly Simon reveals her Parkinson's disease diagnosis and basal cell carcinoma surgery, explaining why she withdrew from the public spotlight.
story: The co-founder of The Michael J. Fox Foundation called it "powerful" to see two Parkinson's patients interacting with one another.
Carly Simon has Parkinson's disease and underwent surgery for basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer.
The "You're So Vain" singer told People magazine in a statement published July 27 why she had recently stayed out of the spotlight.

"It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly," the 83-year-old told the outlet. "Parkinson's is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable. Some days I'm so tired I can't get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work and feel like myself."
MICHAEL J. FOX SAYS GOING PUBLIC WITH PARKINSON'S WAS 'HELL' ON WIFE TRACY POLLAN

On July 27, 2026, Carly Simon told People magazine in a statement that she has Parkinson’s disease and underwent surgery for basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer. "I have not stopped living, and I have not stopped working," she told the outlet. (Jack Mitchell/Getty Images)

"The problems began with arthritis in both knees and one hip," the star shared. "I eventually had all three joints replaced, out with the old and in with delicate bouquets of metal and plastic. After three replacement surgeries, I assumed my difficulty walking was simply an unfortunate and rather ironic part of the recovery process."

According to Simon, her mobility continued to worsen. She struggled to stand from "low chairs and deep couches" without someone offering help. "Overstuffed furniture became my enemy," she recalled. There were periods when she couldn't walk "without considerable help."
Simon knew something was wrong.
WATCH: DEBORAH W. BROOKS COMMENDS MICHAEL J. FOX FOR HIS 'COURAGE' TO LIVE OPENLY WITH PARKINSON'S
It wasn't until she underwent an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic that Simon was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. She soon began treatment to help manage stiffness and other symptoms.
"Parkinson's is usually associated with movement, tremors and balance, but it can affect much more than the body," Simon explained.

"It can bring anxiety, depression, exhaustion and apathy. The apathy is particularly strange. You can find yourself lying there like a starfish drying in the sun, arms pointing in all directions, while nothing inside is telling you to get up, read, watch, write, sing, call someone or do much of anything at all. ... It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list."

Carly Simon performs during the 2017 Tribeca Film Festival Opening Gala premiere of "Clive Davis: The Soundtrack of Our Lives" at Radio City Music Hall on April 19, 2017, in New York City. (Clint Spaulding/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

During this period, Simon was treated for basal cell carcinoma on her face. While surgeons removed the skin cancer, the procedure left her self-conscious about her appearance and reluctant to be seen in public.

"I have always been more critical of my appearance than anyone else could possibly imagine (check out the irony of having written 'You're So Vain'), and this gave my inner critic quite a lot of new material," Simon wrote.

"Between my mobility issues, the Parkinson's diagnosis, the surgery and the emotional effects of it all, withdrawing from public view was the most palatable reaction," Simon said. "If a person is allowed to hibernate during both winter and summer, then I have become an all-season bear."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Recording artist Carly Simon stands for a portrait in New York City on June 18, 2008. She lives on Martha's Vineyard. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Despite her personal struggles, Simon stressed that she has "not stopped living, and I have not stopped working." She quietly worked on a new album, "Comes in Waves," noting that music "has rescued me more times than I can count."
"Working on the music gave shape to days that did not always have much shape," Simon said. "... It reminded me that illness can change your life without becoming the whole of your life."

"I do not consider Parkinson's a gift or a blessing," she said. "It is neither. It is difficult, frustrating and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and now how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential. I am still writing, singing, imagining, laughing, worrying, remembering and occasionally getting trapped in an overstuffed chair."
Carly Simon and Tony Shanahan pose backstage at the 31st Annual Tibet House US Benefit Concert and Gala at Carnegie Hall on March 3, 2018, in New York City. (Getty Images for Tibet House)

"I am deeply grateful to my children, my family, my friends, my caregivers and the medical professionals who have helped me through this," Simon said. "Their love and patience have carried me through days when my own reserves were not enough. I wanted to share this now because so many people have reached out with genuine concern. I am touched by that concern, even when I have not known how to respond."
"These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different. But I am still very much here."
People reported that "Comes in Waves" is Simon's first full-length album since 2008.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Good friends Carly Simon and Jackie Onassis pose for a picture at Bunch of Grapes Bookstore on Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, on Sept. 2, 1989. (Stephen Rose/Getty Images)

Simon, who lives on Martha's Vineyard, made one of her last public appearances in 2019 when she visited SiriusXM Studios in New York City to promote her memoir, "Touched by the Sun: My Friendship with Jackie," which chronicles her once-close bond with former first lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.
People reported that Simon's last public performance was in March 2018 at the 31st Annual Tibet House U.S. Benefit Concert & Gala at Carnegie Hall.

Musician Carly Simon (center) and sisters Lucy Simon and Joanna Simon attend The National Academy of Popular Music's 25th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony on June 1, 1994, at Sheraton New York Hotel and Towers in New York City. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Although Simon was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, she did not attend the ceremony in Los Angeles. The event came weeks after her sisters, Joanna and Lucy Simon, died of cancer one day apart. People noted that Simon survived breast cancer after being diagnosed in 1997.

Olivia Rodrigo performs under a photo of Carly Simon during the 37th Annual Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony at the Microsoft Theatre on Nov. 5, 2022, in Los Angeles. (AFP via Getty Images)

According to the Mayo Clinic, Parkinson's disease is a nervous system disorder that affects movement. Symptoms can include tremors, balance problems, stiffness, slowed movement and slurred speech. Although there is no cure for Parkinson's disease, medications and, in some cases, surgery can help manage symptoms.

Michael J. Fox, who was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 1991, was one of the first high-profile figures to raise public awareness of the disease. The "Back to the Future" star later founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Christopher Lloyd (left) and Michael J. Fox (right) are seen here during the "Back to the Future" reunion panel. (Mike Coppola)

Simon rose to fame with her 1971 self-titled debut album. The Grammy winner is best known for the 1972 hit "You're So Vain" and the James Bond theme "Nobody Does It Better," recorded for the 1977 film "The Spy Who Loved Me," starring Roger Moore as 007.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Friday Night Lights' star Adrianne Palicki says Texas gave her something Hollywood couldn't
summary: Adrianne Palicki reveals how Austin, Texas, gave her creative freedom and community that Hollywood's negativity never could after leaving Los Angeles.
story: Adrianne Palicki told Fox News Digital that Austin, Texas has "heart."
"Friday Night Lights" star Adrianne Palicki found something in Texas that she knew Hollywood would never give her.

During an interview with Fox News Digital at a special fan screening celebrating 20 years of the iconic show — hosted by Plex and ATX TV, Palicki explained that she found "heart," which she did not have while living in the "negativity" of Los Angeles.

"Heart. Not a lot of my friends are actually even in the industry, but it does give us creative freedom and now there's a huge industry starting to pick up there," she began, referring to Austin, Texas. "We're able to make the movies we wanna make."
Adrianne Palicki starred as Tyra Collette in "Friday Night Lights" from 2006 until 2011. (Getty Images)

The actress explained that in LA, it requires a lot of money to make movies. "And in Austin, you can get together with your friends and you can, you know, scrape it up, and you just make whatever you want to make, and I think that's really special," Palicki said.

She explained that she decided to make the move thanks to filming "Friday Night Lights." Palicki told Fox News Digital that after shooting the pilot, she fully moved to Texas and initially would stay with Connie Britton, who played Tami Taylor on the hit show.

"I think getting outside of the element that can be sometimes negative in LA, where we're all vying for the same thing," she said of her decision to move. Speaking of Texas, Palicki said, "It's just a very positive environment and community."

"Friday Night Lights" premiered in 2006 and Plex and ATX TV are celebrating 20 years. Plex and ATX hosted this event as part of a nationwide road trip to celebrate the show’s 20th anniversary. They have upcoming stops in New York and Kansas City.

title: Katy Perry blasts White House for using hit song 'Firework' she sold in $225M catalog deal
summary: Katy Perry blasted the White House for using "Firework" in a TikTok video of military strikes without her permission after selling song in $225 million catalog deal.
story: Podcast host Benny Johnson speaks on the Democratic Party’s next potential presidential candidate on Jesse Watters Primetime.

Katy Perry blasted the White House for using her hit 2010 song "Firework" in a TikTok video without her permission, years after the pop star sold the majority of her music catalog in a reported $225 million deal.
On Thursday, the White House TikTok account shared a video featuring black and white footage of recent military strikes on Iranian targets, timed to the "boom, boom, boom" lyric from "Firework."
"Iran has been warned," the caption read, along with a firework emoji.
POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC'
In an X, formerly Twitter, post that she shared on Saturday, the 41-year-old pop star condemned the inclusion of her song in the clip.

"I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes," Perry wrote. "I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it."
Katy Perry slammed the White House for using her song "Firework" in a military strikes video. (Sergione Infuso/Corbis via Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments," she continued. "To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for."
"My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare," Perry concluded.

The White House's post comes as President Donald Trump's administration remains locked in a tense standoff with Iran following recent U.S. military strikes and ongoing diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
When reached for comment, the White House directed Fox News Digital to an X post by Deputy Assistant to the President and Deputy Communications Director Kaelan Dorr.
WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK AFTER ROBERT DE NIRO, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN TAKE TRUMP SWIPES AMID COLBERT'S FAREWELL WEEK

In a reply to Perry's post, Dorr shared a montage of clips from the music video for the singer's 2012 song "Part of Me" in which the 13-time Grammy Award nominee was seen joining the U.S. Marines and undergoing military training alongside other service members.
"This you?" Dorr wrote alongside the video.

In September 2023, Perry sold her music catalog rights covering her first five studio albums to Litmus Music, a subsidiary of The Carlyle Group, in a deal reportedly worth $225 million. The agreement included her interests in the master recording royalties and music publishing rights for "One of the Boys" (2008), "Teenage Dream" (2010), "PRISM" (2013), "Witness" (2017) and "Smile" (2020).

Released in 2010 as the third single from "Teenage Dream," "Firework" topped the Billboard Hot 100 for four weeks and became one of the biggest hits of her career. The song's success helped "Teenage Dream" tie Michael Jackson's "Bad" as the only albums in history to produce five number one singles.
Perry sold the majority of her music catalog, including "Firework," in 2023 for a reported $225 million. (AP Photo/Chris Pizzello)
Along with "Firework," the sale also encompassed many of Perry's other mega-hit singles, including "I Kissed A Girl," "Hot N' Cold," "Roar," "California Gurls" and "Dark Horse."

Perry is the latest artist to clash with the Trump administration over the use of their songs in official social media posts. Other musicians who have recently objected include Ariana Grande, Kesha, Sabrina Carpenter, Céline Dion, Bruce Springsteen and others.

In June, Grande slammed the Trump administration for using her song "Bye" in a TikTok video depicting Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests, writing in the comments section: "please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. f-- ice."
The White House later fired back at the "Wicked" star in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

"We’ll say this one last time: what’s actually barbaric, inhumane, and heinous are the criminal illegal aliens who have injured and murdered innocent American citizens," White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said.
However, the song was later removed from the video.
Perry is the latest artist to clash with the Trump administration for using their music in social media videos. (Getty Images)

In March, Kesha denounced the White House on social media after it used her 2010 hit "Blow" in a TikTok video showing a fighter jet launching a missile at a naval target, saying the administration was using her music to "incite violence and threaten war."
"Trying to make light of war is disgusting and inhumane," Kesha wrote on X.
The "Die Young" singer said she "absolutely" does not "approve of my music being used to promote violence of any kind."

title: Melissa Gilbert, Michael Landon and more: Where the original 'Little House on the Prairie' cast is now
summary: The Netflix reboot has sparked renewed interest in the 1974 series. Reconciliations, salary disputes and surprising career paths followed the cast.
story: Sidney Greenbush recalls behind-the-scenes memories with the "Little House on the Prairie" cast and explains why she stepped away from acting. Greenbush is the author of a new children's book, "Seven Sisters – The Lantern of Humanity."

The popular new adaptation of "Little House on the Prairie," which began streaming on Netflix earlier this month, has caused a resurgence of interest in the original 1974 television series starring Melissa Gilbert and Michael Landon.
But what happened to the original cast?
The cast of "Little House on the Prairie" is seen in a promotional photo. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Melissa Gilbert
Melissa Gilbert played Laura Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie."  (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images)
Melissa Gilbert is best known for her portrayal of Laura Ingalls in the original series, which she began in 1974 at just 9 years old.
The 62-year-old had already been on shows like "Gunsmoke" and "Emergency" when the show started.
Also serving as the narrator of the show, Gilbert stayed on "Little House on the Prairie" for all nine seasons, until 1983.
BELOVED 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' FACES WAGONLOAD OF 'WOKE' ALLEGATIONS OVER NETFLIX REBOOT
During her time on the show, she made several TV movies, including "The Miracle Worker," "The Diary of Anne Frank" and "Splendor in the Grass."
She also reprised her role in the TV movies "Little House Years," "Little House: Look Back to Yesterday," "Little House: The Final Farewell" and "Little House: Bless All the Dear Children."
Gilbert continued to act after the show ended on dozens of TV movies and she also voiced Barbara Gordon on "Batman: The Animated Series" from 1992 to 1994.

Gilbert also made TV appearances on shows like "Touched by an Angel," "Providence," "7th Heaven" and "Nip/Tuck." She had a recurring role on Hallmark’s "When Calls the Heart," but recently revealed in an Instagram post that she would not be returning to the show. She said she was told that was due to "budget issues."

The news came after her husband Timothy Busfield, who she married in 2013, was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor and one count of child abuse in January. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor.
Busfield has denied the charges and Gilbert has continued to support him, telling ABC in April that he is the "last person in the world who would hurt a child."
"I trust him with my children's lives, with my grandchildren's lives, my nieces and nephews," she added. "He is an honorable, caring, generous human being."
ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE' VILLAIN RETURNS FOR REBOOT WITH WARNING FOR NEW NELLIE
Gilbert also defended the new reboot after she said she’d seen fans debating on social media whether the new version or the original were historically accurate and faithful to the books.
"The short answer is no, neither are entirely accurate to the times nor the books," she wrote in a Substack essay.

After giving several examples of inaccuracies, she wrote: "My hope is that folks realize that these are all perfect examples of dramatic license. Even the real Laura took dramatic license in writing her books. For example, in the book, ‘Little House on the Prairie,’ all three Ingalls girls are older than they were in real life."

She added, "So rather than getting all twisted up in what’s real and what’s dramatized, maybe just sit back and go for the ride the creative minds behind these shows want to take you on. If you like it, stick with it. If you don’t, you don’t have to watch."
Michael Landon
Michael Landon is seen here on "Little House on the Prairie" and in 1990, a year before his death. (NBCU Photo Bank; Photo by Kypros/Getty Images)

Michael Landon, who played Laura’s father Charles Ingalls on the show, began acting in the 1950s, appearing on shows like "Cheyenne," "Suspicion" and "The Rifleman." He was also in the movie "I Was a Teenage Werewolf."
Landon directed many of the show’s episodes and wrote and produced the show.
Before "Little House," he starred as Little Joe Cartwright on the long-running series "Bonanza."
Landon continued to work on several TV movies after the show ended, and he starred as angel Jonathan Smith on the 1984 to 1989 series "Highway to Heaven."
He also reprised his role as Charles Ingalls in four TV movies.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Landon died at 54 years old in 1991, just months after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
Gilbert called Landon a "mentor and father figure" in a Fox News Digital interview in 2024. She said she saw her TV dad a week before he died.
"There were always funny moments with Michael," she said. "Even as sick as he was, he still maintained his incredible sense of humor."

Gilbert frequently posts memories of him on her Instagram, writing earlier this month, "I’ve always felt like the luckiest girl in the world because he chose me to be his ‘Halfpint.’ Working with him was more than formative. I learned most of what I know about our industry from him."
Karen Grassle
Karen Grassle seen as Caroline Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie" and at an event in 2024. (George Hurrell/NBCU Photo Bank; Arnold Jerocki/WireImage)
Karen Grassle, who played Laura’s mother Caroline, was mainly a theater and Broadway actress before landing the role on "Little House."
After the show ended, the 84-year-old continued to act until 2021, starring in the movie "Not to Forget."
Grassle had a contentious relationship with Landon while on the show, which stemmed from a salary dispute in Season 2 and prompted her to leave a year before the show ended.

She formed a special bond with her onscreen children "so they felt comfortable doing scenes with me as their mother," but her relationship with Landon, whom she called an "amazing, multi-talented person," soured, according to People magazine.

"I felt insulted as his co-star on a hit series," Grassle told the New York Post about his refusal to grant her a raise, arguing she should be paid the same as her onscreen children. "I didn’t want to gouge anybody, but I expected a fair wage."
She said Landon also cut her onscreen time during the dispute and made sexist jokes on set.
The actress reconciled with Landon before his death, telling the Post: "I am very grateful that we mended our fences."
Grassle is also very proud of her time on "Little House," calling her character "an incredibly strong woman with a nature full of texture. Her spirit is one to live by."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Melissa Sue Anderson
Melissa Sue Anderson played Laura's older sister Mary Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie." (Bruce Birmelin/NBCU Photo Bank; Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)
Melissa Sue Anderson played Laura’s older sister Mary Ingalls on the show.
The 63-year-old was the only member of the cast to be nominated for an Emmy for an episode about her character going blind.
Two years older than Gilbert when she started on the pioneer show, Anderson had only done a little TV work — including as Bobby Brady’s first kiss — before "Little House."

Anderson made her film debut in the horror movie "Happy Birthday to Me" in 1981 and after the show ended, she made TV appearances on shows like "Hotel," "Murder She Wrote," "The Equalizer" and "The Love Boat."
She met her husband, Michael Sloan, while appearing in the 1980s reprisal of "Alfred Hitchcock Presents." The couple welcomed two daughters and Sloan died in 2025.
Anderson and Gilbert famously didn’t get along.
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' RETURNS AS NEW NETFLIX ADAPTATION AIMS FOR WHOLESOME ENTERTAINMENT
"We were very, very different," Anderson told the Atlanta Constitution-Journal.
Anderson also published a memoir about her time on the show called "The Way I See It: A Look Back at My Life on Little House."
Gilbert felt that Anderson acted like the boss on set.

"From the moment we walked onto that set, Melissa Sue Anderson was the boss of me," she said in an interview, according to Parade. "She took that absolutely seriously. She was two years older than me, which, you know, when you’re 9 and 11 is a big deal."
Gilbert added, "She was tough on me both off and on camera, but on camera especially."

Anderson explained that she was just very shy, telling Harry Brownstone on his podcast last year: "I wish I had been more outgoing so I could have enjoyed it more and been more easygoing about everything."
However, the pair reunited last year at Gilbert’s off-Broadway play "Pen Pals."
"Reconnection with a sister," Gilbert wrote. "Long, healing talks. Lots of reminiscing. Lots of catching up. Lots of laughter and a few tears."
MICHAEL LANDON'S 'LITTLE HOUSE' CO-STAR EXPOSES ACTOR'S WILD ON-SET PRANKS
"Just us Ingalls girls. The best part is, the past is now just that and we can move forward as the sisters/friends we always wanted to be," she wrote.
Rachel Lindsay and Sidney Greenbush
Sidney and Rachel Lindsay Greenbush both played younger sister Carrie Ingalls. (Gary Null/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; David Livingston/Getty Images)
Twins Rachel Lindsay and Sidney Greenbush were just 3 years old when they were cast as younger sister Carrie Ingalls.
Sharing the role for eight years, they chose to leave after the eighth season when they were 12 years old.

"Everybody separated, and I didn’t see anybody," Rachel Lindsay said at a 50th anniversary reunion, according to Entertainment Weekly. "And that was really hard for me personally because I didn’t realize how connected I had been to everybody until years later."

"You make these really deep, intense bonds working with each other every single day, and then when it’s over, you’re just supposed to be like, ‘Okay, that was nice. Bye,’" she told the outlet. "And it’s really hard that way."
Both sisters retired from acting in 1983 to focus on their education.
In 2014, she married Daniel Sanchez, whom she first met when he lived near the set and used to sneak on to hang out with the cast and crew, according to People magazine.
She also has a grown daughter from a previous relationship.
Sidney acted in "Hambone and Hillie" in 1983 and Rachel Lindsay was in an episode of "Matt Houston."
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR REVEALS WILD FRIENDSHIP WITH JIM MORRISON BEFORE WHOLESOME TV FAME
Sidney just wrote a children’s book called "Seven Sisters: The Lantern of Humanity."
"I remember when they were making the movie 'Return to Oz.' My sister made it to the final three girls who were selected," Sidney told Fox News Digital last month.

"They all did screen tests, and for the silliest of reasons, they chose another girl over her," she said. "Of course, we all know there can only be one choice in the end, but it's a lot of pressure for children. So I decided I was going to explore other things because sometimes you go to what they call 'cattle calls,' where there are so many people competing for the same role. The casting directors aren't always nice."
The two sisters were credited as "Lindsay Sidney Greenbush" on the show.
Alison Arngrim
Alison Arngrim played bully Nellie Oleson on "Little House on the Prairie." (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; Arnold Jerocki/WireImage)
Nellie Oleson, the daughter of the mercantile store owners who bullied Laura, was played by Alison Arngrim.
The 64-year-old was just 12 when she began acting opposite Gilbert, saying at the 50th reunion the two of them were "like sisters" on set, according to People.

"It's so completely bonkers," Arngrim said. "Here's Melissa Gilbert and I playing mortal enemies, beating each other senseless all week. And then on the weekends, we'd go to each other's house for a slumber party, and we were hanging out."
She is also the author of "Confessions of A Prairie Bitch: How I Survived Nellie Oleson and Learned to Love Being Hated" and had a one-woman show called "Confessions of a Prairie Bitch."
In 2002, she was honored with the Young Artist Former Child Star Lifetime Achievement Award for her work on the show.
Aside from "Little House, Arngrim also made appearances on shows like "Fantasy Island," "The Love Boat," the TV movie "Life Interrupted" and she recently made a cameo on the "Little House" reboot.
Katherine MacGregor
Katherine MacGregor was gossip Harriet Oleson on the show. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
Katherine MacGregor played nasty gossip Harriet Oleson on the show.
After she died at 93 years old in 2018, Gilbert called her "outspoken and hilariously funny" in an Instagram post.
"A truly gifted actress as she was able to play a despicable character but with so much heart. Her Harriet Oleson was the woman our fans loved to hate. A perfect antagonist," she added.
"The thing people outside of our prairie family didn't know, was how loving and nurturing she was with the younger cast."
Before "Little House," MacGregor acted on shows like "Mister Peepers," "Mannix," "Emergency!" "All in the Family" and "Ironside."
NETFLIX'S 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' ACTOR HOPES NEW SERIES WILL UNITE OLD AND NEW FANS
She was also a successful Broadway actress and she returned to the theater after the show ended. She retired from acting in the early 2000s.
Richard Bull
Richard Bull played Nels Oleson, Harriet's husband and Nellie's father. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
Richard Bull played Nels Oleson, husband to Harriet who, with her, owned the town mercantile store.

Bull began acting in the 1950s, landing parts on shows like "Perry Mason," "Highway Patrol," "The Virginian," "The Fugitive," "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "Gidget," "Gomer Pyle: USMC," "The Andy Griffith Show," "Bewitched," "Mission: Impossible" and "Bonanza" before the show’s run.
He also starred as the doctor on "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea" from 1964 to 1968.
He continued to act until 2011 on shows like "Lou Grant," "Knots Landing," "Hillstreet Blues," "Designing Women" and "ER."
Bull died at 89 years old in 2014.
He also reunited with Landon on three episodes of "Highway to Heaven."
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES
Dean Butler
Dean Butler came onto the show later in the series to play Laura's husband. (NBCU Photo Bank; Albert L. Ortega/Getty Images)
Dean Butler played Laura’s eventual husband, Almanzo Wilder, who came onto the show in the sixth season.
He also appeared on shows like "CHiPs," "Fantasy Island," "Who’s the Boss?" "The Love Boat," "Hotel," and had a recurring role on "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
From 1986 until 1988, he starred on "The New Gidget" as Jeff "Moondoggie" Griffin.

His last acting role was in 2008, and since then he has mainly worked behind the camera as a sports, entertainment and documentary producer, including a docuseries he narrated called "The Little House Phenomenon: A Place in Television History."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Butler, like Gilbert, commended the reboot, writing on Instagram earlier this month: "Something that I love about the program that I think would have been really fun in the original — which we did not do... is the family singing. Writers have rolled in songs that Pa played on his fiddle, and the family is singing along, and they’re doing it beautifully, and this really is the spirit of Laura’s books."
He added that the show is beautifully produced, saying "there is a lot of good stuff going on here."
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Shark Tank' star Daymond John says 'you'll be screwed' if you do this when starting a business
summary: Daymond John reveals his top business advice at Fanatics Fest, explaining why Kevin O'Leary and other entrepreneurs never chase money first.
story: The 57-year-old businessman told Fox News Digital you have to be passionate about whatever business you are starting and shouldn't do it just for the money.
"Shark Tank" star Daymond John is giving fans some blunt advice on how to be successful in business.
When speaking to Fox News Digital at Fanatics Fest, the 57-year-old businessman shared that to have a successful business, you have to build it around "something that you love."

"If you're starting something that you love, you have to want to do it for free. I always say to kids, you know, you got to get paid for what you'd do for free, you'd be able to sell whatever you would buy. So, any business is a great business. Emptying garbage is a great business if you really love it. If you're doing it just for money though, you'll be screwed. Even Kevin O'Leary, you think he does it for money? No, he just likes complicated structures that manage his downside. But at the end of the day, he likes the chess game."
The reality TV star began working at a young age, developing his entrepreneurial spirit before founding FUBU ("For Us, By Us") in 1992 along with three of his childhood friends.
DIGITAL ENTREPRENEUR CREDITS THE WORLD CUP WITH TEACHING ABOUT SOCCER AND BOOSTING HER MONTHLY INCOME
Daymond John advised young entrepreneurs to build a business around something they love and would buy themselves. (Michael Yarish/WBTV via Getty Images)
Now a global fashion brand, the business began with John sewing wool hats and T-shirts himself in his mother's house in Queens, New York.

"First of all, I was frustrated by Timberland, and a couple of other people and brands that 'didn’t make clothes for African Americans,'" he told The Source Magazine. "That was why I initially created FUBU. It was my love of fashion as well and my love for music. And I felt that no longer did we have to have the 'make it and they will come theory' like other designers."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He continued: "I was a designer who actually respected the community I was selling to, and it was fun. It was an exciting time. Hip-hop was young and fresh, and I was just happy to wear the clothes that I was making as well as seeing artists and other people wear the clothes that I was making for them."
WATCH: ‘SHARK TANK’ STAR DAYMOND JOHN SHARES WHAT WILL GET YOU ‘SCREWED’ IN BUSINESS
After turning FUBU into a global fashion brand, John joined the original cast of "Shark Tank" in 2009, alongside Barbara Corcoran, O'Leary, Robert Herjavec and Kevin Harrington.
John was cast on "Shark Tank" in 2009. (Christopher Willard/Disney via Getty Images)
As a shark, John has invested in a number of businesses, helping entrepreneurs get them off the ground. Some of his most famous investments include Bombas and Bubba's-Q Boneless Ribs.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I always look for the person first — before the idea," he told Inc. about his investing philosophy. "I need to know that they are going to get the right information, and not go off and make mistakes without at least trying to educate themselves. I value an entrepreneur I can get behind and trust because I know they are attempting to move forward in life."
While at Fanatics Fest, John told Fox News Digital, "I'm just here being a fan myself." (Disney/Christopher Willard)
While at Fanatics Fest, a Comic-Con style celebration and immersive sports festival, John told Fox News Digital he was looking forward to experiencing everything the festival had to offer as a fan.

"I haven't gotten to see most of it, but for three years in, I mean, this is nuts, right? It's everything from WWE to UFC, to, of course, all the sports stuff, the signing, the trading, all of the celebrities and the sports people here. I'm just here being a fan myself," he said.
