"The one thing that has stopped many unpopular policies since the beginning of 2025 isn’t the Democrats — it is the filibuster," Fetterman wrote in his opinion piece.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: GOP senator unveils BOASBERG Act to stop 'rogue' judges from handpicking Trump cases
summary: Sen. Eric Schmitt's BOASBERG Act would require random assignment of federal cases and bar chief judges from influencing who hears high-profile disputes.
story: Sen. Eric Schmitt, Republican from Missouri, joins Maria Bartiromo to advocate for the impeachment of Judge James Boasberg, labeling him a "rogue judge" due to alleged partisan actions and past rulings.
FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican is planning to curb so-called "rogue" judges, and he is using one of President Donald Trump’s greatest foils in the judicial branch as the launching point.

Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., is planning to introduce the Blocking Overt Attempts at Shopping By Enforcing Randomization Guidelines Act in an attempt to curb judge shopping in federal cases. The bill, shortened to the BOASBERG Act, is named after U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, one of Trump’s main antagonists on the bench.

Schmitt’s legislation, first obtained by Fox News Digital, would broadly require that federal cases be randomly assigned in a bid to limit the ability of judges and litigants to influence who gets to hear and oversee a case.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., is dropping legislation that would require federal cases to be doled out to federal judges at random to prevent so-called "rogue" judges in the Judicial Branch, and it's named after Judge James Boasberg — the GOP’s "poster child" for political forces in the judiciary, according to Schmitt. (Getty Images)

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system," Schmitt said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts."
Schmitt’s legislation adds several guardrails to the selection process for federal cases and gives courts 120 days after enactment to implement them.

It would require the random assignment of federal civil cases, prohibit chief judges from influencing case assignments, require courts to publicly disclose their case assignment practices, create penalties for meddling with or manipulating the assignment process, and require the random reassignment of a case if the Supreme Court intervenes in a ruling.
DC APPEALS COURT ORDERS JUDGE BOASBERG TO HALT TRUMP CONTEMPT PROBE OVER DEPORTATION FLIGHTS

Boasberg, who was first appointed to the federal bench by former President Barack Obama in 2010, has become a flashpoint for Republicans and the White House for his role in several high-profile cases against Trump and his administration during his two non-consecutive stints at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.
It’s caused Trump to call for his impeachment and the Justice Department to file a misconduct claim against him.

Boasberg most recently blocked the State Department from restricting visas for foreign officials and other foreign nationals that the administration has accused of suppressing or helping suppress American free speech.
SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS
President Donald Trump addresses the nation from the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on July 16, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
That latest move is just the tip of the iceberg in a long-running set of clashes between Boasberg and Trump.

Boasberg has been a key player in the administration’s attempt to deport Venezuelan migrants. He tried to temporarily block the administration’s fast-paced deportation of Venezuelan migrants that the White House alleged were Tren de Aragua gang members.
He later ordered the administration that the men had to be returned to the U.S. for violating due process in their removal.

Boasberg also landed the case surrounding "Signalgate," where top members of Trump’s Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance, War Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and then-National Security Advisor Michael Waltz, among others, accidentally included a journalist in their encrypted group message discussing strikes in Yemen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He ordered the administration to preserve any of the messages related to the group chat, but stopped short of requiring that the administration salvage any that may have been deleted.
Schmitt hopes that his legislation will create a new operating standard moving forward.

"The BOASBERG Act prevents judges from forcing their way onto cases and is an important piece of court transparency legislation that will help restore the American people's confidence in our judiciary," Schmitt said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Battleground Democrat flip-flops on conversion therapy after left-wing backlash
summary: Rebecca Cooke reversed her stance on a federal conversion therapy ban after progressive backlash, raising viability questions in the key swing district.
story: Legal and political strategist Katie Zacharia discusses the Supreme Court’s ruling on Colorado’s conversion therapy ban on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
A Democratic House candidate vying to flip a key Republican-held seat is on the defensive after reversing her position on conversion therapy following backlash from the party's left flank.

Rebecca Cooke, a Democratic challenger vying to unseat Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., repeatedly declined to endorse a federal ban on conversion therapy during several forums held ahead of the Aug. 11 primary.

But after drawing criticism from some progressive voters, Cooke reversed course, saying the federal government should prohibit the controversial practice, which often involves mental health professionals offering talk therapy for individuals struggling with their sexual orientation or gender identity.

The issue gained renewed attention when the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Colorado could not enforce a state-level ban on conversion therapy over free speech concerns, sparking backlash from some Democrats.

Demonstrators rally in response to the U.S. Supreme Court's rejection of a Colorado law banning conversion therapy for LGBTQ minors at Stonewall National Monument in New York on April 1, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME

The reversal comes as Cooke appears to be walking a political tightrope on LGBTQ issues in the Trump-friendly swing district, where she must appeal to both Democratic primary voters and the broader electorate.
Before Cooke can seek a rematch against Van Orden, she must first overcome a primary challenge from former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge, who is running to her left.
Asked what lawmakers could do to push back against the Supreme Court ruling at a May forum in La Crosse, Cooke sidestepped the question and said she preferred "local communities having control."
"I’m in favor of that sort of local control when making policies like this," the Wisconsin Democrat said.
Wisconsin’s conversion therapy ban took effect in 2022, while the city of Eau Claire, in Van Orden’s district, prohibited the practice in 2018.
Meanwhile, at a June candidate forum in Platteville, Cooke said "no" when asked if the federal government should pass legislation to ban conversion therapy.
Her answers prompted outrage from some progressive voters.

"I find it interesting that not in one, but TWO forums you said you would leave conversion therapy up to the states to decide," one user wrote on Facebook. "That is not protecting the LGBTQ community."

"I don’t know how you can say ‘Happy Pride’ if you aren’t willing to stand up for people you want to represent in Congress," another account replied. "If you are willing to sell out the LGBTQIA+ community for votes, who is next?"

Rebecca Cooke, candidate for Congress in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, speaks during a town hall hosted by Pete Buttigieg at the La Crosse Center on Jan. 16, 2026, in La Crosse, Wis. (Kayla Wolf/Getty Images)
CHRISTIAN COUNSELORS CHALLENGE WISCONSIN CONVERSION THERAPY BAN AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING
Amid the backlash, Cooke said she "misunderstood" the moderator's question and said she supported a federal ban on conversion therapy in a statement posted on a third-party account after the debate.
During a July forum in Eau Claire, Cooke clarified, "I do not support conversion therapy whatsoever."
Berge, who helped enact Eau Claire’s local conversion therapy ban, was clear throughout the candidate forums in denouncing the practice.
"As a therapist, conversion therapy has no place in our society, in our culture," she said during the June event.
Republicans sharply criticized Cooke’s reversal on conversion therapy bans.
Van Orden's campaign argued Cooke, who counts Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., among her endorsers, flip-flopped on her stance while still trying to "portray herself as a moderate."

"Rebecca Cooke is so desperate to appease the far-left woke mob that Wisconsin voters can’t be sure where she actually stands," Republican National Committee (RNC) spokesman Hunter Lovell told Fox News Digital.

"She’s trying to be one candidate for liberal activists and another for everyone else," he continued. "Whether it’s caving to the far left or scrambling to rebrand herself for the general election, Cooke owes Wisconsinites an answer: Which Rebecca Cooke would show up in Congress?"
Fox News Digital reached out to Cooke for comment.

Cooke, a former Democratic consultant, fundraiser and small business owner, has consistently supported expanding LGBTQ rights during her previous two failed bids for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District.
Rep. Derrick Van Orden speaks before Vice President JD Vance at Pointe Precision in Plover, Wis., on Feb. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)

In her third run for the seat, the repeat candidate is making clear that the Democrat-backed Equality Act — legislation that would make sexual orientation and gender identity protected classes under federal civil rights law potentially affecting women-only spaces and female sports teams — is a "centerpiece" of her campaign.
She is also endorsed by the progressive Human Rights Campaign, which has advocated for sex change procedures for minors, including hormone therapy and puberty blockers.

President Donald Trump comfortably carried the sprawling swing district by more than seven points in 2024, meaning Cooke would likely have to win over a segment of the president’s voters to prevail in November.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Cooke, who significantly outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris, lost to Van Orden in the general election by just under three points in 2024, according to analysis from The Downballot.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the battleground contest as a "toss-up."

title: Russia exposes NATO weapons gap as top commander warns ‘the math is not in favor of the West’
summary: NATO's top transformation commander says the West cannot produce enough Patriot missiles and must redesign its entire weapons industrial base.
story: French Adm. Pierre Vandier said Ukraine has exposed an arsenal that cannot be produced at the scale now required, warning there is "no way to produce 50,000 Patriots a year."

Days after NATO allies committed tens of billions of dollars to new air and missile defenses, the alliance’s top transformation commander warned that the West must fundamentally redesign its weapons and industrial base to withstand attacks at the scale now being demonstrated in Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Today, the math is not in favor of the West," Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation (SACT), told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview following the alliance’s summit in Ankara, Turkey, in early July.
A U.S.-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile is launched during a live-fire exercise at the Chiupeng missile base in Pingtung County on Aug. 20, 2024, Adm. Pierre Vandier ( )
The summit produced commitments to acquire 900 Patriot missiles and invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities throughout five years.
But Vandier argued that simply buying more of the West’s existing weapons will not solve the underlying problem.
TRUMP ENTERS FINAL NATO SUMMIT DAY AS UKRAINE, DEFENSE SPENDING TAKE CENTER STAGE

Russia’s nightly barrages against Ukraine have exposed an air-defense model designed for smaller numbers of incoming threats. The U.S.-Iran conflict has simultaneously intensified demand for the high-end interceptors needed to defeat ballistic missiles, including Patriots and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) that cannot quickly be replaced.
"There is no way to produce 50,000 Patriots a year," Vandier said. "We don’t have the supply chain, and it’s not worth doing that given the cost of the weapon."

Instead, Vandier said NATO needs a layered mix of defenses: cheaper weapons that can be mass-produced to counter waves of drones, while preserving advanced interceptors for ballistic missiles and other sophisticated threats.
A U.S.-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile is launched during a live-fire exercise at the Chiupeng missile base in Pingtung County Aug. 20, 2024. (Sam Yeh/AFP via Getty Images)
THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE

"You need to have attritable, low-cost, mass-produced weapons to just kill the low-cost weapons that are coming by big waves," Vandier said. "And then you need still the exquisite, complex weapons to kill the most complex weapons, as ballistic missiles."

Trump announced at the summit that the United States would grant Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot interceptors, potentially allowing Kyiv to build more of the weapons it urgently needs to defend against Russian ballistic missiles.

But asked whether the announcement changed his assessment that Patriots alone could not protect Europe throughout the next five years, Vandier pointed to a deeper obstacle: Western weapons were designed around an industrial base that no longer exists.
UKRAINE’S BATTLEFIELD IS TRANSFORMING THE FUTURE OF NATO
"The design needs to change," Vandier said. "We are at a moment where some stuff will be redesigned under pressure to be mass-produced."

NATO also is attempting to transform against a threat that is changing in real time. Asked about a recent Russian live-fire exercise on Lake Peipus, between Estonia and Russia, which Estonia’s defense minister assessed was likely practice against Ukrainian-style naval drones, Vandier said Russia has demonstrated an ability to absorb battlefield lessons and adjust "on a weekly basis."
"War — if you do not adapt, you die," Vandier said. "All your brain is about how you outmatch, outpace, outrun the enemy. And so Russia is not that bad at that."
"For NATO now, it’s a question of speed of adaptation," Vandier said. "It’s a mind game."

Ukraine’s defense industry, meanwhile, is increasingly setting the pace for the larger Western manufacturers that once supplied most of its weapons, Vandier said. Ukrainian companies have been able to develop, field and modify systems quickly in response to changes on the battlefield.

President Donald Trump said the United States would send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine during a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in the Oval Office on July 14, 2025. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
"The very agile and fast-evolving industrial base in Ukraine is now giving the pace to the European and Western industry," Vandier said.

But the technological competition is not confined to drones and air defenses. Vandier warned that the collapse of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty has reopened a broader race over long-range missiles in Europe, as Russia and NATO allies seek weapons capable of holding targets farther behind enemy lines at risk.

The 1987 treaty prohibited the United States and Russia from possessing ground-launched missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers. The first Trump administration withdrew from the agreement in 2019 after accusing Moscow of violating it, an allegation Russia denied.

Rescuers conduct search and rescue operations at a multi-storey residential building damaged in a massive Russian missile and drone attack in the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv, Ukraine, on July 2, 2026. Russian forces launched a large-scale attack on the city using strike drones and various types of missiles. Private homes, apartment buildings, an emergency medical substation, and a hotel building were damaged (Kyrylo Chubotin/Ukrinform)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Vandier said the disappearance of those limits has produced a period of "complete strategic instability," with both sides under pressure to develop new capabilities to preserve deterrence.
"The Pandora’s box is open again," Vandier said, "and we’ll try to close it down one day."

title: WATCH: Rand Paul says Fauci lobbied for $1M prize while leading COVID response
summary: Rand Paul claims Anthony Fauci lobbied NIH colleagues to nominate him for the $1 million Dan David Prize while serving as White House medical advisor.
story: Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., is gearing up for a blockbuster hearing with Anthony Fauci and alleged to Fox News Digital that Fauci lobbied members of the NIH to nominate him for a lucrative, $1 million prize.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., wants answers from former chief White House medical advisor Anthony Fauci on why he used his rising fame to lobby colleagues to nominate him for a $1 million prize.

Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, is gearing up for a blockbuster hearing with Fauci, the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), for his role as spokesman and policy craftsman during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ahead of the hearing, Paul dumped over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary, and he told Fox News Digital that one of the issues that would soon come to light during Wednesday’s fight in the Senate was Fauci’s alleged dogged pursuit of a hefty cash prize while serving under former President Joe Biden.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, speaks during a press briefing at the White House on April 13, 2021, in Washington. (Patrick Semansky/AP Photo)

"We have conversations where he's telling other people at the NIH to nominate him," Paul said. "Like, ‘Will you nominate me? I'll write up my nominating background for you, and then you nominate me.’"

"Why would we let — politicians aren't supposed to get more than $50," he continued. "Why would we let a guy that runs a bureaucracy, why would we want him to be allowed to have a $1 million prize? That just boggles my mind."

In 2021, Fauci was awarded the Dan David Prize, a $1 million award disbursed by the Israel-based Dan David Foundation headquartered at Tel Aviv University. Per the rules of the award, 10% of the prize was meant to be designated for academic scholarships in Fauci’s field.
LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION NEARS FINISH LINE AS WORLD LEADERS GATHER TO HONOR HIM

The foundation said in a statement at the time that as the pandemic unraveled, Fauci "leveraged his considerable communication skills to address people gripped by fear and anxiety and worked relentlessly to inform individuals in the United States and elsewhere about the public health measures essential for containing the pandemic’s spread."
Despite advising seven presidents and serving at the NIH since the 1980s, Fauci was a career civil servant who never required Senate confirmation.
Strewn across the pages of Fauci’s diary are several instances, particularly in the early stages of the pandemic, that show an individual with a keen understanding of his role in the media.
FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., talks with reporters in the Senate subway on Dec. 9, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
In May 2020, for example, Fauci wrote that a "Big front page article [about] me appeared in the Washington Post."

"Very flattering. The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable," he said. "It is not [hyperbole] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable [persons] in the world."
And in another entry shortly after, Fauci noted that the Trump White House was "very upset" about his meteoric rise in the media.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, is sworn-in before testifying before the House Oversight and Accountability Committee Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic at the Rayburn House Office Building on June 3, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
When asked about Fauci's close eye on the media and whether that might have colored his portrayal of the virus, Paul was unsure.
"I mean, he wouldn't be the first person in Washington that publicity went to his head," Paul said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Trump welcomes Netanyahu to White House as raging Iran war threatens to sour US-Israel relationship
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu plans to present Trump with intelligence alleging Iran is expanding nuclear activity at its Pickaxe Mountain site, reports say.
story: 'Fox & Friends' co-hosts react to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's calls to have him arrested under International Criminal Court warrants. Netanyahu addressed Mamdani's remarks during an interview on 'Sunday Morning Futures,' confirming plans to travel to Washington to meet President Donald Trump and attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.
President Donald Trump will welcome Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to the White House Tuesday for talks that could shape the next phase of the U.S. standoff with Iran.
A political shadow is cast over the visit, however, amid renewed calls from the far-left to arrest the Israeli leader.

"Every meeting between Prime Minister Netanyahu and President Trump has carried drama and historic weight, but this one comes as the Middle East stands at a genuine crossroads," Shurat HaDin Law Center President Nitsana Darshan-Leitner told Fox News Digital of the upcoming sit-down.

"The decisions made by these two leaders in Washington will have far-reaching repercussions and will determine not only the next chapter in confronting Iran, but whether the region moves toward lasting stability or slips back into dangerous and chaotic escalation," added Darshan-Leitner.
NETANYAHU TO VISIT TRUMP AT WHITE HOUSE, ATTEND 'DEAR FRIEND' LINDSEY GRAHAM'S MEMORIAL SERVICE
Netanyahu and Trump meet to speak about key issues at the White House, including the war in Gaza and tariffs on April 7. (Getty)

Netanyahu is in Washington, D.C., to attend the funeral service of Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., whom he has called a dear friend not just to Israel, but to himself. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also in D.C. for the funeral of the late senator and is using the opportunity to meet with Trump.
The high-stakes talks between the world leaders come as Israel continues to press for a tougher Iran strategy, while Trump is weighing whether to resume major strikes against Iran.

"He's been a great wartime prime minister," Trump told reporters Wednesday, speaking of Netanyahu. "We worked with each other very closely. And we went through a very big thing. We did a big thing together."
The Israeli leader’s visit has stirred controversy over Israel’s handling of Gaza as well as its approach to Iran.
MAMDANI GOES BACK ON CAMPAIGN PROMISE, SAYS NYC CAN'T ARREST NETANYAHU
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) greets Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as he arrives at the White House on September 29, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called on the federal government to carry out the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant ahead of a possible Netanyahu visit to the Big Apple for the United Nations General Assembly in September.
Former Mayor Bill de Blasio defended Mamdani’s call to have Netanyahu arrested, stating the Israeli leader is "fomenting hate."

The relationship between longtime allies Trump and Netanyahu — who is often referred to as Bibi — appeared to face a rare rift over their differing views in the two countries' handling of the conflict with Iran.
TRUMP CONFIRMS ‘CRAZY’ NETANYAHU CLASH AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER PUSH TO HOLD FIRE ON HEZBOLLAH TERRORISTS
Trump admitted that he called Netanyahu "f---ing crazy" in a heated phone call over Israel’s military operations in Lebanon.

"So many in the media attempt to portray deep rifts between the President and the Prime Minister while they need to project unity and strength," Darshan-Leitner explained to Fox News Digital. "History will likely remember this meeting not simply for what was discussed behind closed doors, but for the course it set for the region — and perhaps the world — for years to come."

Netanyahu is expected to present Trump with intelligence in their meeting on Tuesday alleging Iran is expanding activity at its Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site and is not negotiating in good faith over its nuclear program, according to the New York Post, citing a source in Jerusalem.

President Donald Trump hosts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Mar-a-Lago on Dec. 29, 2025, with talks addressing Iran’s renewed threats and potential progress on the next phase of the Gaza peace framework. (Israel Government Press Office)
Trump delayed planned U.S. military strikes against Iran for several days while emphasizing that the United States remains prepared to launch a "massive attack," if necessary.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump said Monday Washington is engaged in "good talks" with Iran, but warned that if negotiations fail, the U.S. would resume military action.

"From the future of Iran’s nuclear ambitions, to the security of U.S. bases, to the ownership of the Strait of Hormuz and the freedom of global maritime commerce, the stakes extend far beyond Israel’s borders," said Darshan-Leitner. "This is one of the rare moments when diplomacy and deterrence must move in lockstep."
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Fauci privately took credit for COVID-19 lockdowns despite public denial, newly exposed diary entries reveal
summary: Anthony Fauci's private diary reveals he personally convinced Bill de Blasio to close New York City schools, bars and restaurants in March 2020.
story: Dr. Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal his fixation on personal fame during the COVID-19 pandemic. Critics point to his diary's lack of focus on public health terms versus personal accolades, raising questions about his priorities and the pandemic's origins.

Despite denying on multiple occasions during and after the COVID-19 pandemic that he personally recommended lockdowns, excerpts revealed from Dr. Anthony Fauci's private diary prove a clear contradiction.

In a March 15, 2020, entry in the diary, which begins with "BIG DAY!" written in red letters, Fauci, then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID) recalled a striking conversation he had with then-New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio.

"I spoke with Bill de Blasio (Mayor – NYC) and convinced him based on what I was saying publicly and my conversation tonight to close the NYC schools (he had already decided based on what I was saying on TV)," Fauci revealed in his private notes.

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee about the COVID-19 response in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4, 2021. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"I had a similar call with Ann O’Leary, the [Chief of Staff] of Gov. Gavin Newsom of California," this particular entry went on. "Ann said that based on my TV appearances today and yesterday, the Governor has decided to close the schools in California as well as the bars and restaurants."
But seven months later, in an Oct. 16, 2022, interview with ABC News' Jonathan Karl, Fauci denied any involvement in inspiring lockdowns.
"Let's go back and look at the transcript. We said we should try as best as we possibly can to keep the children in school," Fauci said. "Nobody plays that clip."
"They always come back and say, 'Fauci was responsible for shutting schools down.' I had nothing to do [with it]!" he insisted at the time.
EXPOSED FAUCI DIARY SHOWS HE ESTIMATED COVID-19 DEATH RATE TO BE MUCH LOWER THAN WHAT HE TOLD CONGRESS
In 2022, he told The Hill that he "didn't recommend locking anything down," clearly going against his own privately recorded entries.
On January 9, 2024, years after the end of lockdowns ended, Fauci testified the same thing before the House Oversight Committee.
"I did not close the schools," he said, according to the hearing transcript. And it became the widespread situation where I became a political target."

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, throws out the ceremonial first pitch prior to the game between the New York Yankees and the Washington Nationals at Nationals Park on July 23, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)
Fauci recommended to government leaders lockdown measures besides just closing schools, which he would also later deny.
INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES
In the March 15, 2020, diary entry, Fauci, once the nation's leading infectious disease expert, said he directed de Blasio to close the city's bars.
"I went on to tell him he should close the bars and restaurants in NYC. He said that he would base this on my recommendation," Fauci wrote.
Five days later, he said he told the mayor to close all of New York City.

"Also, had phone call with [Mayor] de Blasio who wants to go to 'shelter in place for the entire city.['] He is asking my advice since Gov. Cuomo is pushing back. I advised DeBlasio [sic] to go ahead and do it. I will try to speak with Cuomo," the entry said.
2020 Democratic presidential candidate and New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio visits FOX Business Network’s "Bulls & Bears" in New York City on Aug. 13, 2019. (Steven Ferdman/Getty Images)
On March 29, 2020, Fauci recounted a tense meeting with President Donald Trump, who he described as "incorrigible."

The goal of the meeting was to get the president to extend lockdowns after the initial "15 days to stop the spread" period, which began on March 16 of 2020 — about a month after the first case of COVID-19 was recorded in the U.S.
"At the end of the day, it was a good outcome since we convinced him to go with 30 day (sic) instead of ending the mitigation prematurely, which I feel would be a disaster," Fauci said.
In a November 28, 2020, diary entry, he recalled lending support to a Los Angeles County health official who wanted to lock the county down.

"Got call last night from Mark Ghaly (Deputy Director for Community Health for the LA County Dept of Health Services). He has called me several times for advice," the diary says. "Frantic call saying that they are surging in LA County and very soon hospital beds will be overrun. He wants to do a 3 weeks shutdown of the city to 'stop the surge' and wants my support since there is a large pushback to locking down. I agreed to support him."

A signboard reminds people of the face-covering requirement as pedestrians wear facemasks due to the coronavirus in Los Angeles, California, on November 12, 2020. (Photo by FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images)
But again in 2022, when he joined The Hill's "Rising" podcast, Fauci denied responsibility for lockdowns.

"Well, you know, again, first of all, I didn't recommend locking anything down," he claimed. "You're asking me questions. You're talking about the CDC is the public health agency that uses their epidemiologists and their science-based approach to make recommendations..."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Despite his own denials, Fauci himself told CBS news in the midst of the 2020 chaos that he was behind the lockdowns.

"When it became clear that we had community spread in the country, with a few cases of community spread — this was way before there was a major explosion like we saw in the northeastern corridor driven by New York City metropolitan area — I recommended to the president that we shut the country down," he said on Oct. 7, 2020.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Soros network rebuilds progressive prosecutor push after string of election losses
summary: Soros family pumped more than $1 million into PACs backing progressive prosecutors for 2026 elections, despite recall elections and defeats that removed dozens of district attorneys.
story: Congressman Wesley Hunt, a Republican from Texas, strongly condemns the Democratic Party's anti-police rhetoric and 'defund the police' movement. Hunt argues that leftists believe criminals are victims, leading to increased crime rates and unsafe communities for the most vulnerable. He emphasizes the need for strong law enforcement, contrasting it with the left's demonization of police.
The Soros family has pumped more than $1 million into political action committees (PACs) dedicated to electing progressive prosecutors this election cycle, campaign finance documents show.

While some predicted that Soros-backed district attorneys would become a thing of the past after sustaining a string of defeats between 2022 and 2024, records suggest that the liberal family is giving their criminal justice reform crusade another go. Democracy PAC, now run by George Soros’s son Alex, pumped roughly $1.7 million into the federal and non-federal arms of the Justice & Public Safety PAC between March 2025 and April 2026, according to public records.

The renewed spending signals that the Soros network is rebuilding its effort to shape local criminal justice policy ahead of the 2026 elections, despite a voter backlash that removed or replaced dozens of prosecutors linked to its funding.

By directing significant resources to Justice & Public Safety PAC, the family is positioning the group to again influence races where decisions on bail, charging and sentencing can drastically reshape public safety.
REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY
Alex Soros, son of billionaire George Soros, revealed he voted for Zohran Mamdani for New York City mayor. (Chris Kleponis / AFP/Getty Images)

The Soros family, led for decades by billionaire investor and philanthropist George Soros, has spent heavily on charitable foundations and political committees to advance liberal candidates and human rights worldwide, including efforts to make society more equitable through criminal justice reform and other initiatives. The elder Soros transferred control of the family’s roughly $25 billion philanthropic and political network to his son Alex in 2023.

Justice & Public Safety PAC is the organization responsible for providing financial backing to a number of prosecutors who have since become infamous in conservative circles, according to Influence Watch. Among these are former Alameda County, California, District Attorney Pamela Price, former Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon, Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, former St. Louis Circuit Attorney Kim Gardner and former Cook County, Illinois, State Attorney Kim Foxx.

Critics charge that these prosecutors fail to incarcerate dangerous members of society, leading to increased crime. Supporters, meanwhile, maintain that addressing the root causes of crime, such as poverty and inequality, will stop offenses before they occur and that harsh punishments for criminals incentivizes recidivism.

Gascon, for one, attracted criticism for ordering his prosecutors not to pursue many sentencing enhancements, which can result in criminals being put away for longer, and for drastically reducing the number of misdemeanors tried by his office, according to the Los Angeles Times. He faced significant internal dissent as crime rates climbed, with rank-and-file prosecutors voting nearly unanimously to support a recall effort against him, Politico reported.

Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascon speaks during a press conference about the facts surrounding the fatal shootings of two El Monte police officers at the Hall of Justice in Los Angeles on Tuesday, June 21, 2022. (Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images)
AS SOCIALIST MAYOR BATTLES ICE, SEATTLE POLICE AND CRIME VICTIMS SAY REPEAT OFFENDERS ARE TERRORIZING THE CITY
Krasner, meanwhile, has been denounced for presiding over a historic homicide spike in his city while he reduced prosecutions.
These controversies were not without consequences for Soros-backed prosecutors.

Of the 25 district attorneys with links to Soros that appeared on the ballot in 2024, 12 were either defeated or recalled, including Gascon. Sean Kennedy, the Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund’s policy director, told Fox News Digital at the time that, of the 75 Soros-linked prosecutors his organization had identified since 2022, 50 had either left office or been replaced with more moderate officials.
DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

Hungarian-born U.S. investor and philanthropist George Soros addresses the assembly on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum (WEF) annual meeting in Davos on May 24, 2022. (Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty Images)
Justice & Public Safety backed a progressive prosecutor in Virginia’s 2025 election, providing some potential insight into the kinds of candidates it will bankroll as Election Day 2026 approaches.

The committee spent six figures backing the candidacy of Norfolk Commonwealth Attorney Ramin Fatehi, campaign finance records show. Conservatives criticized Fatehi over his opposition to cash bail, his resistance to prosecuting crimes like shoplifting and his participation in a coalition of prosecutors aiming to prosecute federal immigration agents.

"The old-fashioned view about public safety was not taking into account externalities. It was focused on the idea of crime as an evil unto itself," Fatehi said in a 2021 interview. "Where I part ways is in recognizing that crime is a symptom. It’s a symptom of structural racism, of systematic community disinvestment, of redlining, unequal school policy, the lack of jobs, lack of transportation, a lack of opportunities, intergenerational barriers to wealth building, the disinvestment in the treatment of the mentally ill."

Soros himself similarly argued in a 2022 essay that progressive prosecutors can improve public safety by using resources to address the root causes of crime rather than resorting to jailing criminals for long periods of time. Supporting his claim, he wrote that "black people in the U.S. are five times as likely to be sent to jail as white people," which is "an injustice that undermines our democracy."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Soros family has other sources of cash available to fund its political goals ahead of 2026, including the Open Society Foundation, a 501(c)(4) advocacy group that brought in nearly $160 million in 2024, according to tax documents.
The Open Society Foundation, the Soros family’s philanthropy, did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital Monday.

title: Far-left Senate hopeful explains ‘ogre on a pike’ remark after getting torched by his own party
summary: Abdul El-Sayed refused to apologize for his "ogre on a pike" remark, revealing he was targeting John Fetterman, not primary rival Haley Stevens.
story: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., was the target of his controversial "ogre on a pike" remark during the candidates’ final primary debate but did not take it back. (Credit: WJBK)

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, declined to apologize Monday night for his "ogre on a pike" metaphor after critics from both parties condemned the leaked remark as violent and, in some cases, sexist.

Pressed during the final primary debate before next week's election, over whether he regretted the rhetoric, El-Sayed defended the substance of his comments before revealing whom he had been referring to — and it was not primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

"I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman," El-Sayed said, accusing the Pennsylvania Democratic senator of getting elected on one set of values before "completely throwing those values in the mud."
GRETCHEN WHITMER ENDORSES MODERATE HALEY STEVENS IN TIGHT UPCOMING SENATE PRIMARY

The controversy stemmed from comments El-Sayed made during a recent Zoom meeting with donors, Politico reported, adding that El-Sayed was discussing how to use his victory in Michigan’s upcoming Aug. 4 primary and the November election to build a national platform to move the Democratic Party further left and support future primary challenges, such as against Fetterman.
U.S. Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA) walks through the Senate Subway during the Senate War Powers vote on April 22, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

"Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed said, according to audio obtained by Politico. While El-Sayed did not name Stevens in the recording, some Democrats interpreted the remark as referring to her. Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who has endorsed Stevens, called the remark a "violent, vulgar" threat and said candidates should be working to lower the political temperature.

Neera Tanden, a former Biden administration official who returned to leading the left-wing think tank the Center for American Progress, connected the remark to broader accusations of sexism that have roiled the primary. "Calling your female opponent an ogre you want to put on a pike is not beating the rap that this race has some serious sexism," Tanden wrote on X.
SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS

El-Sayed did not apologize for or retract the metaphor. He instead argued that senators should be willing to challenge colleagues who fail to act according to the values on which they campaigned. The progressive candidate then pivoted to accuse the United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC, of running repeated attacks against his character on Stevens’ behalf. He invoked his wife, mother and two daughters while rejecting accusations that his rhetoric toward women had been disrespectful.
Michigan Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at The People V. The Powerful rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

"I was raised by strong women," El-Sayed said, arguing that claims he was sexist because he had criticized former first lady Michelle Obama in a years-old opinion piece and challenged Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the 2018 gubernatorial primary were "inconsistent with the truth."

Stevens responded by highlighting other comments attributed to El-Sayed during the leaked donor call, including attacks involving Whitmer, former Sen. Debbie Stabenow and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was in the race with El-Sayed and Stevens before dropping out earlier this month.
"Only he can account for saying that Whitmer is bought and paid for, or that no one cares about Debbie Stabenow, or that Mallory McMorrow isn’t smart enough," Stevens said.
She later delivered a pointed response to El-Sayed’s clarification.
"Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre," Stevens said.

Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and former Wayne County Health Department Director Abdul El-Sayed are facing off in the August 4, 2026, Democratic Senate primary in the Great Lakes battleground state. (Getty Images)
MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT MALLORY MCMORROW DROPS OUT OF SENATE RACE WEEKS BEFORE PRIMARY
Meanwhile, Stevens' campaign spokesperson, Arik Wolk, accused El-Sayed of resorting to personal insults and focusing on his national political ambitions rather than Michigan.

"Abdul continues with personal insults and making this race about his personal political ambitions and the other 49 states," Wolk said. "Haley is focused on getting things done for Michigan, and only Michigan."

Republicans also took advantage of the remarks. RNC Research characterized El-Sayed’s debate response as a "double down" on calling Fetterman an "ogre," while Michigan Republican strategist Dennis Lennox argued that El-Sayed’s candidacy was "about propelling the hard Left’s ascent nationally."

The "pike" imagery has triggered political controversy before. In 2020, former Trump White House strategist Steve Bannon said he would place the heads of Dr. Anthony Fauci and then-FBI Director Christopher Wray "on pikes" outside the White House as a warning to federal officials.

X, then-Twitter, suspended Bannon’s podcast account following backlash over the remarks, while Facebook and YouTube removed the video they were included in, citing policies addressing violent or incendiary content. Bannon later maintained that he had been speaking metaphorically — similar to El-Sayed.
Steve Bannon speaks at the National Conservatism Conference in Washington D.C., Sept. 3, 2025. (DOMINIC GWINN/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Earlier that year, a separate "head on a pike" controversy erupted during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial after CBS News reported that an unnamed Trump confidant said Republican senators had been warned, "Vote against the president and your head will be on a pike."

Then-House impeachment manager, now Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., repeated the report on the Senate floor while stressing, "I don’t know if that is true" and "I hope it is not true." Republican senators immediately disputed the account, with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, saying she knew of no senator who had been threatened by the administration and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, said of Schiff’s remark about the alleged comments: "That’s when he lost me."

"Not only have I never heard the ‘head on the pike’ line, but also I know of no Republican senator who has been threatened in any way by anyone in the administration," Collins told reporters at the time.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Prominent Holocaust museum challenges Mamdani with offer in response to claims about 'genocide' in Gaza
summary: Holocaust Museum Chairman Jeff Miller invited Zohran Mamdani to visit and learn what genocide actually means after the NYC mayor's repeated use of the term.
story: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani delivered remarks from Gracie Mansion on St. Patrick’s Day. (Credit: NYC Mayor's Office)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is yet to publicly respond to an invitation from a prominent Holocaust museum to visit in order to "truly understand" what "genocide looks like" as he faces criticism from the Jewish community for repeatedly using that label to describe the situation in Gaza.

"You keep using the word ‘genocide’ when talking about Israel," Jeff Miller, chair of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, posted on X on Friday, inviting Mamdani to visit the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C.

"If you truly want to understand what genocide looks like, as Chairman of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, I would be happy to personally arrange a tour of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum for you."

Miller was responding to a post from the UJA-Federation of New York expressing grief over a pair of recent stabbings in New York City carried out by an attacker who allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" during the attacks. Authorities say one of the victims is Jewish, and the attack is being investigated as a hate crime.
JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a rally in New York alongside 1199SEIU members and immigration advocates after the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can revoke protections for Haitians and Syrians. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Miller’s post went on to say that "words matter especially from elected leaders" and that "rhetoric that demonizes Israel and the Jewish state has consequences."

"I hope you are simply ignoring the impact of your words and not purposely trying to normalize antisemitism," Miller wrote. "My invitation is sincere. Come to the Museum. Learn what genocide actually means."
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office multiple times inquiring whether the mayor intends to take Miller up on his offer but did not receive a response.
SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said his administration is exploring whether the city has legal authority to arrest Netanyahu if he visits for the U.N. General Assembly. (Ronen Zvulun/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Miller told Fox News Digital that he felt an "obligation" to speak up and that he would be "happy" to personally walk Mamdani through the museum.

"If the mayor wants to repeatedly invoke that word, I invite him to come with me to the Holocaust Museum and confront what genocide actually looked like: the systematic attempt to annihilate an entire people," Miller said. "If he does not want to come to our museum, he should visit Rwanda or another place whose people have endured genocide and listen to survivors."

Miller added that Mamdani is free to "criticize the Israeli government" and disagree with policies, "but there is a profound difference between legitimate criticism of a government and rhetoric that demonizes the world’s only Jewish state and helps normalize hostility toward Jews."
Miller’s invitation was celebrated by many on social media, including Republican Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who posted on X that he hopes Mamdani takes the offer.
MAMDANI'S LATEST NETANYAHU REMARKS DEEPEN CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH LEADERS

People participate in a "Climate Justice Means Free Palestine" rally outside Citibank headquarters in New York City on June 18, 2024. Protesters carried pro-Palestinian signs and climate justice messaging during the demonstration. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"The US Holocaust Memorial Museum — where I proudly serve on the Council — is an important institution that shows the truth about what happened," Scott wrote. "I urge anyone visiting Washington, DC to stop by. "
"The @NYCMayor Mamdani should take up the Chairman’s offer for a tour of the Holocaust Museum so he understands what is genocide," billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X.

Mamdani has faced intense criticism for his position on Israel since jumping into the mayoral race last year and since taking office, he has often angered the Jewish community with comments calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and repeatedly accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza after the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people," Mamdani said last week in a video announcement that he did not have the authority to arrest Netanyahu in accordance with an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant, a warrant the United States does not recognize.

"He is responsible for the killing of more than 73,000 people, for the maiming of tens of thousands of children as those who survive undergo amputation without anesthesia. For the targeting of neonatal hospitals and maternity care centers, denying newborns even the chance to live. For the countless people he starved as he blocked food and humanitarian aid from reaching them. For the gunning down of hundreds of aid workers and journalists."

title: Lindsey Graham's final mission nears finish line as world leaders gather to honor him
summary: Lindsey Graham's Russia sanctions bill faces a key Senate vote Tuesday night, hours after his funeral at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C.
story: Shannon Bream discusses with Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Katie Britt their bipartisan bill aimed at sanctioning Russia. Sen. Shaheen emphasizes the urgent need to pressure Vladimir Putin, while Sen. Britt highlights the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's clear-eyed stance on Iran.
As Washington, D.C., prepares to say its final goodbyes to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, his last legislative crusade is inching closer to the finish line.

Graham, who died suddenly at the age of 71 earlier this month, will begin the first part of his final journey home to South Carolina in Washington on Tuesday, when lawmakers and world leaders will gather to pay tribute to the longtime lawmaker.
He will get two celebrations of his life in Washington on Tuesday, first in the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in the morning and then at a private funeral service at the National Cathedral.
TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN
Sen. Lindsey Graham speaks during a briefing on Aug. 12, 2024, in Kyiv, Ukraine. (Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

The services in Washington, D.C., which will be followed by funeral services in Graham’s home state of South Carolina, will close the loop on a life in politics that saw the longtime lawmaker grow from humble beginnings behind his parents’ bar to becoming a leader in national security concerns and foreign policy.

His impact on the world stage will draw several to the services in Washington, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The latter is set to speak with lawmakers Tuesday morning as the Senate prepares to move on Graham’s passion project: inflicting bone-crushing sanctions on Russia in response to the war in Ukraine.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., quoted Graham in relaying the significance of the sanctions package moving forward and the impact it would have on his legacy.

"To quote Senator Graham, ‘It's a big effing deal. We all did well. We all did good,’" Blumenthal told Fox News Digital. "Those were among the last comments he made to me. Neither of us knowing, you know, that he was going to pass, but it is a profoundly significant part of his legacy."
"It's a huge achievement for him," he continued. "And I'm very proud to be, you know, his partner in that effort."

Blumenthal and a growing bipartisan group of senators have revamped the legislation once more, including changing the name to honor Graham, a move pushed by his sister and newly appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C.
LINDSEY GRAHAM'S SISTER CARRIES ON LATE SENATOR'S WORK, BECOMING SOUTH CAROLINA'S FIRST FEMALE SENATOR
But the work is not done, he said.
"It's going to be a very important part of his legacy, and it is a tribute, a fitting and appropriate tribute to him," Blumenthal said. "I hope it passes. We're not there yet."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up the sanctions package, which now includes sanctions against Iran, for a vote last week. Lawmakers are expected to get a chance to move the legislation through a key procedural hurdle Tuesday night, hours after Graham’s service at the National Cathedral.

Thune, who has spoken with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and expected Democrats to buy into the package, was hopeful that the first challenge would go well, but acknowledged that there were some lawmakers who had issues with the bill.
"I hope to, you know, the motion to get on it will be a very big bipartisan vote," Thune said. "And if it is, I think that will at least set up a path to get it done."
'A BIG EFFING DEAL': GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION MOVES FORWARD AFTER HIS DEATH

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks at a podium split with an image of Russian President Vladimir Putin crossing himself at an Orthodox Easter service. (Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea via Reuters; Alexander Zemlianichenko, Pool/AP Photo)

Many of the core aspects of the legislation, which had its own stops and starts on its journey through the Senate, are the same: sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian officials and Russian military leaders, up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports, tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy, like China and India.
It also gives President Donald Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions.

Key changes to the newly unveiled package include adding a "national interest certification" for Trump’s sanction waiver authority and incorporating sanctions on the myriad ships and tankers that comprise Russia’s "shadow fleet" hauling energy exports under the radar.
Passing the sanctions package would, as Blumenthal noted, be emblematic of Graham’s career in Washington.

And Rep. William Timmons, R-S.C., who grew to become a close friend of Graham’s, recalled the dozens of rounds of golf the pair played together in an interview with Fox News Digital shortly after Graham’s death.
He remembered Graham as someone who, if he considered you a friend, always encouraged you to keep going. It was service to the country, however, that was his prime focus, Timmons said.
"I just think that he was very much singularly focused on public service, whether it was the military or in Congress or as a senator," Timmons said. "It literally was his entire life."

title: Wearable patch vibrates when danger is nearby
summary: NC State researchers built a solar-powered wearable patch with six sensors that vibrates against your skin using distinct haptic alerts for each hazard.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Your phone can warn you about bad weather or heavy traffic. However, some dangers cannot wait for you to notice a notification. A hazardous gas may already surround you. Contaminated water may look perfectly normal. By the time you unlock your phone and check an alert, you could have already spent valuable time near the threat.

Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable patch that takes the phone out of that warning process. The device detects environmental hazards, then vibrates directly against your skin.
Different vibration patterns tell you which hazard the patch detected. Meanwhile, a related version gives robots their own form of chemical awareness.

SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS

Researchers developed a wearable patch that detects hazardous gases and water contaminants, then warns users with vibrations directly against the skin before they check a phone. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A wearable warning you can feel immediately

The square patch is slightly smaller than a driver's license. That makes it compact enough to attach to clothing or place directly against the skin. Inside, a microcontroller acts as the patch's brain. A small battery powers the system. Six sensors monitor the surrounding environment for potential hazards.

The researchers designed the sensors to detect threats in the air and contaminants in water. Examples include dangerous gases and heavy metals. Once the patch detects a hazard, a tiny actuator creates a vibration against your skin. That physical alert could be harder to overlook than another phone notification.

"If you're coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible," said Erim Uzunoğlu, the paper's first author and a Ph.D. student at NC State. The research appears in the scientific journal Device.
Why the patch uses vibrations instead of phone alerts

Environmental sensors already exist. Many can send a warning to your smartphone. However, that approach depends on you noticing the alert. Your phone could be in a pocket, buried in a bag or silenced during work.

A physical vibration removes that extra step. The warning reaches your body as soon as the sensor detects a potential threat. Still, the researchers found that adding a small vibrating motor was not enough. The sensation had to feel strong and distinct without becoming uncomfortable.

To solve that problem, they created tiny textured surfaces between the motor and the skin. These surfaces resemble miniature patterns of raised bumps. By changing the size and spacing of the bumps, the team adjusted how each vibration felt. As a result, the alert became easier to notice. The design could prove helpful in loud environments where an audible alarm might disappear into the background.
Different vibration patterns identify each hazard

The patch does not use the same buzzing sensation for every warning. Instead, it produces a separate haptic sequence for each hazard. One pattern might signal a dangerous gas. Another could warn about a contaminant in water.

This creates a small tactile language between the patch and the person wearing it. Therefore, you may understand the type of threat without checking a display. In proof-of-concept testing, the patch successfully detected the targeted substances. It also triggered the appropriate vibration immediately.
However, people would need time to learn what each pattern means. Clear training would become especially important in workplaces where several hazards may be present.
Solar cells help extend the battery life

A wearable safety device offers little protection when its battery dies halfway through the day. To reduce that risk, the researchers placed thin-film photovoltaic cells on the patch's exterior. These cells collect solar energy while someone wears the device.

The solar cells work alongside the internal battery. At the same time, the sensors use relatively little power. During testing, that combination kept the device operating for around 24 hours. That running time could cover a full work shift. However, real-world performance would depend on sunlight, sensor activity and how someone wears the patch.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

A new wearable sensor uses distinct vibration patterns to alert users to environmental dangers, while a companion system gives robots the ability to detect chemical hazards. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Researchers give robots a chemical warning system

As the team developed the wearable patch, the researchers began considering another question. Could a robot use the same tactile warning system? That idea led to an electronic skin, also called e-skin.

The robotic version places the sensor patch over a piezoelectric layer. When the patch vibrates, that movement creates an electrical signal. The robot can read the signal and identify the vibration pattern. It can then respond to the detected hazard without waiting for a wireless message.

During testing, researchers placed the e-skin on quadrupedal robots. When the robots detected chemical hazards, they changed direction and followed a safer route. This system could help robots explore locations that may be unsafe for people. It could also let a machine respond when wireless connections become unreliable.
Why the robot e-skin could be important

Most robots rely heavily on cameras and digital instructions to understand their surroundings. Yet a camera cannot always identify a dangerous gas or invisible contaminant. The e-skin gives a robot another way to sense risk. More importantly, it turns the chemical warning into a physical signal within the robot's body.

That direct connection could support faster decisions. The robot would not need to transmit sensor data to a remote computer before responding. For example, a robot could inspect an industrial site while watching for leaks. It could then stop or change direction when it encounters a dangerous substance.
However, this work remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Researchers will need to test the system across harsher conditions before it can support high-risk missions.

Many experimental wearables rely on highly specialized components. Those custom parts can increase costs and slow production. In contrast, the researchers built most of this patch and e-skin with components that are already available. Only a few elements required custom engineering. That could make the technology easier to scale.

The sensor array is also modular. Developers could remove sensors that are unnecessary for a certain environment. They could then add sensors for hazards tied to a specific job or location. A water-quality worker would need a different setup than someone inspecting an area for chemical leaks.
What this means to you

You cannot buy this wearable hazard detection patch yet. Still, the research shows how safety alerts could move beyond screens and speakers. A vibration against your skin may reach you faster than a notification on your phone. That could become especially valuable when every second affects your exposure.

The technology may eventually help people who work near chemicals or inspect questionable water supplies. It could also support emergency teams entering places where the air may be unsafe. However, several questions remain. Researchers must determine how the patch performs after repeated wear and exposure to harsh conditions. They will also need to reduce false alarms and make each vibration easy to recognize. Comfort will play a role too. A safety patch only works when people are willing to wear it throughout the day.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Scientists at North Carolina State University created a smart patch that could help workers recognize dangerous chemicals through touch instead of smartphone notifications. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

A warning can only protect you when it reaches you in time. This wearable patch brings the alert directly to your skin instead of relying on a phone that you may never check. The separate vibration patterns are especially clever. They could tell you which danger is nearby before you even look at a screen. Meanwhile, the robot e-skin gives machines a physical way to recognize chemical threats and move away from them. That could eventually keep people farther from hazardous areas. The next challenge will be turning a successful laboratory prototype into something durable, comfortable and dependable enough for daily use.

title: What your internet provider, websites and advertisers see
summary: Your internet provider, websites and advertisers can track your browsing activity even without you posting online. Here's how to limit what they see.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.
Most people assume that if they are not posting on social media or sharing personal information online, they are staying relatively private. Unfortunately, that isn't how today's internet works.

Every time you browse the web, multiple companies can collect information about you. Your internet provider can monitor certain parts of your online activity, websites can gather data about your visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles based on your browsing habits.
The good news? Knowing what others can see is the first step toward protecting your privacy.

Internet providers, websites and advertisers can collect information about your online activity, even when you use private browsing. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What your internet provider can see when you browse
Your internet service provider, or ISP, acts as the middleman between your devices and the internet. Every website you visit and every online service you use passes through its network.

If you are not using a VPN, your ISP can generally see which websites you are connecting to, when you are online, how much data you are using and your approximate location based on your IP address. Encrypted websites, which begin with "https://," help prevent your provider from reading the contents of most web pages or messages. However, your ISP can still often see that you connected to a certain website in the first place. That information alone can reveal a lot about your interests, routines and habits.
What websites can learn from your visit

Even if you never create an account, some websites can still learn quite a bit about your visit. They can identify your IP address, estimate your location, determine what device and browser you are using and record which pages you viewed.

Some websites also use analytics tools, tracking pixels and advertising scripts to understand how visitors interact with their pages. These tools can show what links you clicked, how long you stayed and which content got your attention.

In some cases, this information may also be shared with advertising or analytics companies. That is one reason you may see ads that seem closely connected to something you recently searched for, viewed or clicked.
ARE APPLE DEVICES SPYING? WHAT YOUR IPHONE TRACKS
Private browsing keeps your history off the device after you close the window, but it does not hide your activity from websites or internet providers. (Neil Godwin/Getty Images)
Why private browsing does not make you invisible
Private browsing tabs, also known as incognito mode in some browsers, can be useful. They help prevent your browser from saving your local browsing history after you close the window.

However, private browsing does not make you invisible online. Websites can still see your visit while you are on their pages. Your internet provider can still see many of the sites you connect to. If you are using a work, school or public network, the network owner may also be able to monitor certain activity.

Private browsing is better thought of as a local privacy tool. It helps hide activity from someone else using the same device later, but it does not fully hide you from websites, advertisers or your internet provider while you are online.
How to reduce what others can see

You cannot eliminate online tracking entirely, but you can make it harder for companies to collect information about you. Start by reviewing your browser's privacy settings. Turn off unnecessary website permissions, such as location, microphone and camera access for sites that do not need them. Consider using a privacy-focused browser or search engine that collects less personal data.

You can also check out these 11 easy ways to protect your online privacy for more ways to limit online tracking. You should also limit how much personal information you share online. The more details you provide across websites, apps and accounts, the easier it becomes for companies to connect your activity. Most importantly, consider using a VPN.
How a VPN helps protect your browsing activity

A VPN, or virtual private network, encrypts your internet traffic before it leaves your device. Instead of your internet provider seeing which websites you are connecting to, it sees an encrypted connection to the VPN server. That makes it much harder for your ISP to build a browsing profile based on your online activity.

A VPN can also help protect your information on public Wi-Fi networks and mask your IP address from websites, advertisers and other third parties. However, a VPN does not stop every type of online tracking. Websites may still recognize you when you log in to an account, use the same browser or share personal details.
A solid VPN makes this process easier by offering apps for computers, smartphones, tablets, smart TVs and routers. That allows you to protect multiple devices with one account.

A VPN can encrypt your internet traffic and mask your IP address, but it cannot stop every form of online tracking. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)
Quick online privacy checklist
The next time you go online, remember these steps:

Kurt's key takeaways

The internet is built around data, and several companies can collect information every time you browse. Internet providers can see where you are connecting, websites can monitor visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles over time. You cannot disappear completely, but you can reduce what others learn about you. A few privacy-minded habits, combined with a trusted VPN, can help you take back more control of your online activity.

title: Your home is empty. Do burglars already know?
summary: Burglary crews linked to Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce break-ins used public schedules and data brokers to target homes while owners traveled.
story: Retired LAPD lieutenant Jeff Wenninger explains how criminals exploit obituaries, routines and public clues to time home break-ins and what families can do to reduce risk.
In Argentina, authorities recently arrested three Chilean men wanted in the U.S. in connection with a South American theft group accused of burglarizing the homes of professional athletes.

Federal prosecutors linked the group to break-ins involving Kansas City Chiefs stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce, Milwaukee Bucks player Bobby Portis and other athletes. Two of the suspects were also arrested in connection with a burglary at the home of tennis legend Juan Martín del Potro in Argentina.

According to prosecutors, the group identified targets through publicly available schedules and location information, then struck while athletes were away or playing games. Separately, the FBI has warned that international theft groups surveil homeowners to learn their routines and advises travelers to avoid announcing vacations on social media.

Online criminals can research your address, family, travel plans and estimated property value without ever driving down your street. Here's how criminals piece together those digital clues and what you can do to make your home harder to target.
ALLEGED BURGLARY CREW THAT TARGETED PATRICK MAHOMES AND TRAVIS KELCE HOMES ARRESTED IN ARGENTINA: REPORT

Alleged members of a South American theft ring pose with stolen valuables. Federal investigators say the group targeted professional athletes while they were away competing in games. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida/Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images)

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages.
