Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our spam-stopping checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING
Scammers are impersonating LastPass with fake policy emails that lead users to a fraudulent DocuSign page and suspicious software download. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
LastPass phishing scam starts with a routine policy email

The phishing email comes from hello@lastpassnewsletter.com. Its known subject line reads, "Action Required: Review Updated LastPass Security Policies." Inside, the message claims LastPass has made service policy changes. It mentions enhanced SaaS monitoring. It also claims administrators can reset master passwords and that the admin console has improved.

Those details make the email sound like a real company notice. However, the sending domain belongs to the attackers. LastPass says lastpassnewsletter[.]com has no affiliation with the company. The email includes a Review & Access Terms button. That button creates the next layer of the trap.
Fake LastPass page sends you to a DocuSign lookalike

Clicking the button sends you to lastpasscompliance[.]com. The landing page copies the look of DocuSign and claims a document is ready for review. That choice makes sense from a scammer's perspective. Many people receive electronic signature requests at work or while handling personal paperwork. A familiar layout can lower your guard before you inspect the web address.

We have seen the same trust trick in other fake DocuSign email scams. The brand name gives the request a sense of legitimacy, even when the sender and domain do not match. LastPass says Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Cloudflare classified the phishing site as malicious. The page also prompted visitors to download software that claimed to work on Windows and macOS.

LastPass was still investigating the download when it published its warning. Therefore, you should treat the file as dangerous and avoid opening it. The site also displayed a live support chat box, although it was unclear whether the chat worked. The malicious page had gone offline by the time the campaign was reported. However, attackers can quickly replace blocked domains with new ones.
Similar Bitwarden emails widen the warning

LastPass users are not the only targets. Bitwarden customers have received similar messages from hello@bitwardennewsletter.com. Those emails directed recipients to bitwardencompliance[.]com. The matching format suggests attackers may be reusing the same campaign structure across password manager brands.

That matters because password manager customers present an attractive target. One stolen master password could put many saved accounts at risk. Multi-factor authentication may still block access, depending on your security settings.

A password manager remains valuable protection. In fact, autofill can help expose a fake website because the manager should recognize the legitimate domain. You can compare current options in our guide to the best password managers for 2026 at cyberguy.com
LastPass users have faced several phishing lures in 2026

This campaign follows other LastPass-themed phishing attempts from earlier this year. In January, fake messages warned that users had only 24 hours to back up their vaults before maintenance. Then, a March campaign used fabricated email threads about unauthorized account access.

Both approaches relied on urgency to push people into acting before they verified the message. The new compliance notice uses a calmer approach. It looks like paperwork rather than a crisis. That may make it especially effective because policy updates feel normal and boring.
REDHOOK ANDROID MALWARE CAN QUIETLY HIJACK YOUR PHONE
Ways to stay safe from the LastPass phishing scam
The fraudulent page impersonates DocuSign and prompts visitors to download suspicious software for Windows or macOS. (LastPass)
A few careful steps can keep one convincing email from turning into a much larger problem.
Delete the message or report it as phishing. Do not reply. Avoid opening its links or downloading the file it offers.
Use the official LastPass app or type lastpass.com into your browser. Check for account notices after you sign in through the trusted route.

Lookalike domains often add a trusted brand name to words such as "newsletter" or "compliance." Check the website address before the first slash. A legitimate LastPass address should end in lastpass.com, such as support.lastpass.com, rather than merely containing the word "LastPass."

A password manager may refuse to fill your credentials on a fake domain. Treat that as a warning. Do not copy and paste the password to get around it. Instead, close the page and access your account through the official app or website.

Use a trusted device and go directly to LastPass. Change the master password immediately. Then review your vault for unexpected activity, as LastPass recommends. Next, change passwords for sensitive accounts stored in the vault if you see signs of access. Start with email, financial accounts, cloud storage and social media. Use a different password for every account.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS
The scam relies on polished security notices, familiar branding and misleading web addresses to lower users’ defenses. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Do not open software offered by a security notice you reached through email. If you already opened the file, disconnect the affected device from the internet. Then use strong antivirus software to inspect it. Our current best antivirus protection guide at cyberguy.com can help you compare tools that block malicious websites and dangerous downloads. It also covers protection against malware. You can also follow these steps after you clicked a suspicious email and entered information.

Enable multi-factor authentication for your password manager and other important accounts. An authenticator app or security key can add a barrier if someone steals your password. However, never approve a login request you did not initiate. A second security step only helps when you treat unexpected prompts as a warning.

Scammers often use information from data broker sites to make phishing emails feel more personal. That could include your phone number, home address, relatives or past employers. A data removal service can help find and remove some of that information from people-search websites. It will not secure a compromised password manager, but it may give scammers fewer details to use in future attacks. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com
Forward questionable LastPass-branded emails to abuse@lastpass.com. LastPass says no one from the company will ever ask for your master password.
Kurt's key takeaways

What makes this scam dangerous is how normal the email looks. Most people expect password manager alerts to sound urgent. This one arrives dressed up as a boring policy update, which may make you less likely to question it. The biggest red flag is the web address. A company name inside a domain does not mean the company owns it. Before entering a master password or downloading anything, close the email and open the password manager directly. Your master password protects everything stored in your vault. Treat any request for it like someone asking for the keys to your house.

title: Robot bird swims underwater then flies away
summary: MIT and EPFL researchers built an 8.8-ounce robotic bird that flies, dives underwater and launches back into the air using only flapping wings.
story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor meets Saronic CEO Dino Mavrookas to unveil the future of modern warfare with an exclusive look at autonomous drone boats. These innovative vessels are capable of military rescues without putting service members in danger, marking a significant milestone. Mavrookas emphasizes the ability to build thousands of these cost-effective, complex mission-ready ships, including the new 52-foot Mirage.

Watching a diving bird vanish beneath the water can feel almost unreal. One moment it cruises through the sky. Seconds later, it swims after prey before returning to the air. Around 100 bird species can move between those two environments. Engineers have found that natural ability incredibly difficult to recreate at a small scale.

Now, researchers at MIT and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne, known as EPFL, have built a robotic bird that can complete the entire journey. The 8.8-ounce robot flies, plunges into water and swims below the surface. Then it launches back into the air using the same set of flapping wings.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Researchers say the $300 robot marks the first bird-scale machine to complete an air-to-water-to-air cycle using flapping wings alone. (Raphael Zufferey)
According to the research team, it marks the first bird-scale robot to complete that full cycle through flapping motion alone. The research appeared in the journal Science.
Free live CyberGuy class: Sick of Spam? Join us July 22

Join us TODAY, Wednesday, July 22, at 1 PM ET for a free CyberGuy Live class that will help you cut down on robocalls, spam texts, junk email and other unwanted messages. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our spam-stopping checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
How this robot bird swims underwater and flies

Most amphibious robots use separate systems for air and water. This mechanical bird takes a simpler approach. The robot relies on flapping wings instead of propellers. It also completes its water launch without legs or a complicated wing-folding mechanism.

That design presents a major engineering problem. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so wings face far greater resistance once they enter the water. To handle that dramatic change, the robot adjusts its flapping speed. Its flexible wings also change shape as the surrounding pressure increases.
Flexible wings help the robot move through water

In the air, the robot can flap its wings up to 11 times per second. Underwater, its flapping rate ranges from 0.1 to 6 times per second. Meanwhile, water pressure can bend the wings by as much as 90%. That flexibility shortens the effective sweep of each stroke and reduces the load on the motor.

The same wings become more effective for flight once the robot reaches the air. Researchers also made the machine neutrally buoyant. As a result, it neither rises nor sinks on its own while underwater. That balance helps conserve battery power because the robot spends less energy fighting buoyancy.
Why the robot bird's water takeoff matters

The hardest part begins when the robot tries to leave the water. It completes the transition in under one second using about eight to 10 wingbeats. However, the maneuver requires a careful combination of wing flexibility, tail placement and launch angle.

Researchers found that moderately flexible wings worked best. A rigid wing struggles to adapt underwater, while excessive flexibility reduces the force needed for takeoff. The tail also needs to remain short and close to the body. Otherwise, it can drag through the water and pull the robot back down. An exit angle near 70 degrees produced the strongest results. A flatter approach creates too much tail drag. A nearly vertical launch can make the robot tip backward into the water.
ZELENSKYY ANNOUNCES 'THE FUTURE IS HERE' AFTER WAR'S FIRST ALL-ROBOT CAPTURE
Scientists envision future versions of the robotic bird monitoring waterways, collecting samples and observing marine wildlife. (Raphael Zufferey)
What the robot bird can teach scientists

The machine also gives scientists a new way to study real diving birds. Tracking the movement of a live bird beneath the surface can be difficult. With a robot, researchers can adjust one feature and measure how that change affects performance.

For example, many diving birds reduce their wingspan while swimming. Researchers have often connected that behavior with lower energy use. The robot's results suggest that shorter underwater strokes may instead help birds increase speed.

The team also compared the machine's propulsion efficiency with that of real birds. Both fell within a Strouhal number range of 0.2 to 0.4, which researchers associate with efficient movement. However, body size can change the launch strategy. Heavier diving birds may use their legs to help push away from the water, while this lightweight robot relies entirely on its wings.
Why the robot may choose flying over swimming

The robot's most efficient travel mode depends on the distance ahead. According to the team's data, flying uses less energy once a journey extends beyond roughly 51 feet. For shorter trips, staying underwater may make more sense.

Water creates heavy resistance, so swimming becomes increasingly costly over longer distances. A future robot could use that difference to plan its route. It might swim toward a nearby target, surface and then fly to a more distant location.
How a $300 robot bird could monitor waterways

The prototype costs around $300 in materials and uses parts that researchers can source commercially. The team also released open CAD files for the project. That could allow universities and other builders with access to a 3D printer to reproduce the design.

Eventually, the robotic bird could help scientists monitor waterways and coastal environments. Researchers imagine launching it from shore or a boat. It could fly toward an area of interest, dive to collect a sample and then return with the data.

Potential missions could include taking measurements near an iceberg or observing marine wildlife from a safer distance. Flapping wings may also offer practical advantages in those environments. They avoid exposed high-speed propeller blades and could produce less noise around animals. Underwater, flexible wings may tolerate contact with debris better than rigid propellers.
INSIDE CHINA’S AI ‘WOLF PACK’ DRONES BUILT WITH TAIWAN CONFLICT IN MIND
MIT and EPFL researchers created a robotic bird that can fly, dive underwater, swim and launch back into the air using flexible wings. (Raphael Zufferey)
What the robot needs before real-world missions

The current prototype still relies on human control during key parts of its journey. Researchers manually launched the robot during several tests. Timers or basic triggers also activated parts of its diving and swimming behavior.

Autonomous navigation represents the next major step. The robot would need to recognize its surroundings and control each transition without human assistance. Salt water creates another hurdle. Testing has focused on fresh water, so future versions will need stronger protection against corrosion. Longer range and improved endurance would also make the robot more useful outside controlled experiments.
What this means to you

You probably will not see robotic birds patrolling your local beach anytime soon. Still, this project shows how future drones could reach places that traditional flying machines struggle to explore. A single robot could gather information above the water before taking measurements below the surface. That flexibility could reduce the need for separate aircraft and underwater vehicles.

The low material cost also matters. Smaller research teams could experiment with the design without investing in an expensive custom platform. As navigation and battery performance improve, machines like this could make environmental monitoring more accessible.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stands out here is how much work the researchers get from one flexible set of wings. The robot changes its flapping speed, while the wings naturally bend to handle the resistance underwater. The launch back into the air makes this more than another bird-inspired drone. Pulling off that transition requires the right wing stiffness and a carefully controlled exit angle. The prototype still needs autonomous controls and better protection for saltwater. Even so, its $300 material cost and open design could give other researchers an affordable foundation to build on.

title: Nolan Wells mystery deepens as email indicates teen drank heavily before vanishing
summary: A newly released Marine Patrol email listed 18-year-old Nolan Wells’ alcohol intake as “heavy” during the search for him after he disappeared on a boating trip to Horn Island.
story: 'Crime Stories with Nancy Grace' host Nancy Grace discusses the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old found dead after a July 4th boat trip. Grace scrutinizes the investigation, pointing out the discovery of deep red subcutaneous tissue on Wells' occipital bone and the suspicious absence of his lungs and throat when the body underwent a second, independent autopsy.

The mysterious death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells has taken another turn after a newly obtained document listed the missing teen's alcohol intake as "heavy" as authorities searched for him on Horn Island over the Fourth of July weekend.
The document, a July 5 Mississippi Department of Marine Resources Marine Patrol email obtained by Fox News Digital, was sent to the U.S. Coast Guard as authorities searched for Wells.
Along with his physical description and last known location, the email lists "Alcohol intake: Heavy," but does not identify the source of that information.
Wells, an Ole Miss freshman from Jackson, Mississippi, disappeared while on a boating trip to Horn Island with friends. An extensive multi-agency search ended July 6 when his body was discovered.
SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

A newly released Marine Patrol email listed 18-year-old Nolan Wells’ alcohol intake as "heavy" while authorities searched for him after he disappeared during a boating trip to Horn Island. (Christine Wonsley/Facebook)
Authorities have not publicly identified a cause or manner of death, and the Mississippi State Medical Examiner's autopsy and toxicology results remain pending.
The newly reported details come days after a private autopsy commissioned by Wells' family concluded his cause and manner of death were "undetermined pending investigation."
NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

During a July 22 news conference, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said an area of "red discoloration" was found on the back of Wells' head but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed the independent autopsy, could not determine a cause or manner of death pending further investigation.
"Crime Stories with Nancy Grace" host Nancy Grace later discussed the findings on her show, where she raised additional questions about the investigation.

She pointed to what she described as deep red tissue beneath the skin at the back of Wells' head and said the independent pathologist did not receive Wells' lungs or throat when conducting the second autopsy.
Grace also questioned whether those findings could be significant but emphasized that she did not know what caused Wells' death and noted there were "many accidental possibilities."

Nolan Wells' body was found July 6, but both the official and independent autopsies have yet to determine how he died, while questions remain about discoloration on his head. (Jackson County Sheriff's Department via Facebook)
"There is deep, red, subcutaneous tissue" on the back of Wells' head, Grace said, adding that the discoloration was localized rather than consistent with postmortem blood pooling.
Grace then questioned why the lungs and throat were unavailable during the independent examination.

"When the second autopsy got the body, the lungs and the throat were missing," Grace said. "I understand why they took the lungs to determine if he had drowned, but why was the neck missing? What about the interior of the throat sparked the initial medical examiner's concern?"
She stressed that those questions remain speculative until investigators release additional findings.
"I don't know," Grace said. "There are many accidental possibilities."

The Jackson County District Attorney has defended the investigation amid growing public scrutiny, saying authorities are following standard procedures and awaiting forensic testing before drawing conclusions.
Authorities have not announced whether foul play is suspected.

title: Supreme Court denies stays for two Florida death row inmates, clearing path for rare double execution
summary: The Supreme Court denied stays of execution for two Florida death row inmates, clearing the way for the state's first double execution since 1964.
story: The Justice Department is recommending the return of firing squads and other execution methods for federal inmates convicted of heinous crimes, fulfilling a President Donald Trump's campaign promise to prioritize victims over serious offenders.
The U.S. Supreme Court denied stays for two Florida death row inmates scheduled to be executed Tuesday, clearing the way for the state to execute the 11th and 12th inmates this year.
The court denied two separate requests for stays in the planned executions.
Former police officer James Duckett, 68, had been scheduled to die at noon on Tuesday, but the execution was delayed awaiting results of the stay requests before the Supreme Court.
THOMAS UNLOADS ON COURT FOR HELPING CONVICTED MURDERER BUT IGNORING 'LAW-ABIDING CITIZENS'
Duckett, according to local media reports, was executed by lethal injection and pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m.

summary: Richard Stevenson allegedly had a BAC of .236 and was going 80 mph in a no-wake zone when his pontoon struck a couple's boat on the Fox River.

An intoxicated boater with a history of driving under the influence decapitated a woman after he crashed into her boat while going 80 miles per hour over the weekend, prosecutors said.

title: Miami Secret Service agent charged in near-deadly fraternity hazing, officials say
summary: A Secret Service agent allegedly served as "dean of pledges" during Kappa Alpha Psi hazing sessions that left two victims needing emergency care.
story: A man whose son died during a 2017 fraternity hazing ritual at Penn State University warned students and parents of the ills of the practice in an interview with Fox News Digital, saying anyone could become a victim.

A U.S. Secret Service agent has been arrested and charged with five felony counts, including attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, after allegedly being involved with hazing "rituals" that left two victims with life-threatening injuries.
Marquez Pinder, a 29-year-old special agent with the Miami Field Office, was ordered to be put on house arrest with a GPS tracking device.

Pinder held the title of "dean of pledges" during four, hours-long hazing sessions for a Miami chapter of the Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, according to an affidavit filed with the Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit of Florida. In that role, Pinder was allegedly involved in the hazing of two prospective members of the fraternity.
SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO
Marquez Pinder was arrested by the Sweetwater Police Department after allegedly being involved in a near-deadly hazing. (Miami-Dade Corrections)

According to court records, the two victims were "paddled" and struck with "canes" by Pinder and two other fraternity members. One victim’s concern was "dismissed" by the fraternity when he reported "urinating blood" during the first hazing session, records show.
Days later, the man had to be intubated at a hospital while receiving "critical care to prevent further physical deterioration and death," a law enforcement officer reported in a sworn statement.

The other victim was treated for "blackened" and "necrotic" tissue on his buttocks from the beating, court records show. "Substantial portions of skin and soft tissue" needed to be surgically removed, and he received "extensive skin grafts to cover the areas," according to an affidavit.
A drone view shows the downtown skyline in Miami, April 16, 2025. Marquez Pinder is a special agent with the Secret Service's Miami Field Office. (REUTERS/Marco Bello)
AMERICA'S TOP PARTY COLLEGE HIT BY ANOTHER SEX ATTACK WEEKS AFTER BRUTAL CAMPUS RAPE CASE

His "mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted," a law enforcement officer wrote. And without emergency medical care, "his injuries would have resulted in renal failure leading to death."
The alleged hazing occurred every day April 1-4 at two different residences in Miami-Dade County, court records show.

During the meetings, the two victims were tested with questions about the fraternity and its history, according to the affidavit. Victims told law enforcement officers that when they failed to answer a question correctly, they were placed in what they called a "stress position," the affidavit shows.
RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

They described the "stress position" as a half-squat with one arm pointed forward. While in that position, the victims said they were "struck on their buttocks with a paddle." One of the victims said that, before the hazing, he was told that "if he ever felt that he was reaching his physical limit," he should tell Pinder, his "dean of pledges," officers reported. He said he was told that indications of reaching that limit might include urinating blood or feeling that he was going to pass out, according to the affidavit.

Investigators reported they’d reviewed messages between fraternity members about the need for cleaning supplies to "mop up sweat and blood" from the hazing. After four days of "testing" to become members of the fraternity, one victim sought emergency medical treatment because his "health continued to deteriorate, and he began to suffer from vomiting, fevers, and immense pain on his buttocks," officers reported.

Marquez Pinder, who works in the Miami Field Office, has been employed with the U.S. Secret Service since September 2023, an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Pinder is currently on administrative leave. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service)

Pinder now faces five felony charges, including two counts of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, two counts of attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon and one count of hazing with a deadly weapon.
Jared James and Elijah Dyous, who allegedly helped in the hazing, face the same charges, court records show.
Jared James faces five felony charges after allegedly hazing two prospective fraternity members. (Miami-Dade Corrections)

Elijah Dyous was arrested in an alleged Miami hazing incident. (Broward County Sheriff's Office)

"The Secret Service remains committed to accountability, professionalism, and integrity, and any misconduct will be addressed swiftly and appropriately upon completion of the investigative and judicial process."

title: Dv4d case: Teen's parents knew of relationship with pop singer before chainsaw dismemberment, testimony says

story: The rising recording artist David Burke, known as D4vd, is accused of murdering and dismembering a 14-year-old girl just two days before his first album dropped.

The parents of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old girl found dead and dismembered in a Tesla belonging to aspiring singer David "D4vd" Burke, had an ongoing relationship with her accused killer that her parents knew about, according to court testimony.

They took steps to separate the two, prosecutors have said, including taking her phone away and calling police when she ran away from home. At one point, he allegedly paid a high schooler $1,000 to deliver her a new phone, according to prosecutors.

And Celeste's sister reportedly went with her and Burke on a trip to Las Vegas. In some text messages, Celeste told Burke she was 16 and 18 years old.

The judge ultimately accepted the prosecution's case and cleared a path to trial. Burke could face the death penalty if convicted, although California has a moratorium on carrying out capital punishment. Prosecutors have not yet made the decision on whether they will seek it.

summary: Savannah Guthrie's emotional Instagram video may signal a new line of communication as she appears to appeal directly to her mother's kidnapper.
story: Savannah Guthrie issued a new plea on Instagram to those who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, in a video posted July 27, 2026. (Credit: @savannahguthrie/Instagram)

Savannah Guthrie's plea Monday may signal a "new line of communication," coming as she appealed directly to her mother's kidnapper, more than 25 weeks after the 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie vanished from her Arizona home.

She made the emotional plea on Monday to her Instagram account, saying her family is "in agony" and "will never stop looking for her." on Tuesday, NBC's Erin McLaughlin reported that the new message may have been in response to a new line of communication.

"It's not clear why Savannah decided to release this message now, but it could be a response to a potential new line of communication. Experts say the language appears to be pointed at whoever committed the crime, though law enforcement have not provided any public updates in the investigation recently," McLaughlin said.
In Monday's video to followers, Savannah Guthrie urged her mother's kidnappers to "Do the right thing now."
NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

Savannah Guthrie, right, has made a new public plea to the person who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, center, from her home outside Tucson, Ariz., left, on Feb. 1. (Getty Images/Fox News Digital)

"Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her," she said. "I'm coming on today with a very specific message. It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts. The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place," Savannah Guthrie said. "I truly believe it is never too late to do right thing. Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us. No matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Savannah Guthrie greets a security guard as she leaves the Today show at Rockefeller Plaza on Thursday, March 5, 2026, in New York. (Photo by Charles Sykes/Invision/AP) (Charles Sykes/Invision/AP)

Savannah Guthrie wasn't on the "Today" show on Tuesday, as she's filming for NBC's new prime-time TV game show, "Wordle." She previously said in June that "I'm not involved in our coverage, but I can't pretend I'm not here."
Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos said his agency is still combing through DNA and video evidence.
"We have so much DNA to sort through. We have so much in terms of video evidence to look at. So I'm still positive that we're going to resolve this," Nanos said.
A federal source close to the Nancy Guthrie investigation told Fox News that Savannah Guthrie was in communication with law enforcement about the video, which was her first message in weeks.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "Today Show" live from Australia. (Photo by Don Arnold/WireImage)
The family is asking anyone with information to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI and claim a reward of over $1 million.
A separate reward is available for information leading to an arrest, and tips can be submitted anonymously through Tucson's Crime Stoppers affiliate at 520-88-CRIME.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

SEND US A TIP
An undated photo of Nancy Guthrie and Savannah Guthrie provided by NBC. (Courtesy of NBC)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jason Pack, a retired FBI agent, told Fox News Digital Savannah Guthrie's wording stood out to him, but cautioned that only investigators have the full picture:

The ask changed. For six months, the family asked for a person, in phrases like "bring her home" and "return her to us," Pack said. This week, Savannah Guthrie said, "Tell us where to look for her." According to Pack, "where to look is not the same as bring her back," though he stressed he would not speculate on what the shift means.

The audience narrowed. In February, the family cast wide on purpose, addressing "whoever has her, or knows where she is," Pack said. This week's message reads as if written toward a single person, he said, pointing to the line, "I know that you have tried to do things the right way." Six months in, Pack said, the family "may believe they know more about who is listening."

A line that reads like a receipt. Pack said he kept returning to the phrase "We have done our part," calling it five words with no accusation in them. He described it as landing "like a receipt," a statement that the family had held up its end.

What is missing. Every prior appeal carried an action item, whether the reward or the anonymous tip line, Pack said. This one asks the public to "tell us," meaning the family directly. "That is a departure," he said, "and departures are worth marking."

title: Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband details ‘big spiral’ as expert says one part ‘scared me’ in mom’s murder trial
summary: Patrick Clancy testified about his ex-wife's mental health spiral on Seroquel and her intrusive thoughts about harming their children before the killings.
story: Margaret McLean, a former prosecutor and Boston College law instructor, discussed Patrick Clancy’s testimony in his ex-wife’s murder trial.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Patrick Clancy, the father of three young children strangled inside their Massachusetts home, became the first witness Monday in his ex-wife’s murder trial, offering jurors a harrowing account of the mental health decline he witnessed before their deaths.

He was the first witness called in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, who faces murder charges in the deaths of the couple's three children in January 2023. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately, while defense attorneys contend severe mental illness drove her actions.
Patrick described watching his then-wife fall into a "big spiral" after she began taking Seroquel, testifying that she lost weight, became severely depressed and began expressing suicidal thoughts.

"Awful," he said when asked how Lindsay was doing physically after starting the medication. "That was really where her big spiral started. She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time."
LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

Patrick Clancy took the stand Monday and described watching his wife fall into a "big spiral" before she allegedly strangled their three young children inside the family’s Massachusetts home. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
Patrick also testified that Lindsay told him she was experiencing intrusive thoughts about harming their children, although she denied having a plan and said the thoughts disturbed her.
"I never saw Lindsay harm the kids," he told jurors.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Monday, July 27, 2026. His ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, is on trial for the murder of their three children. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Margaret McLean, a former criminal prosecutor and trial attorney who teaches law at Boston College’s Carroll School of Management, said Patrick’s measured delivery did little to conceal the anguish of a father being forced to retrace the months preceding his children’s deaths.

"I think his demeanor on the stand is really quite clinical. He’s telling it as it is," McLean told Fox News Digital. "You can see the anguish within this man’s eyes, his facial expressions. You can tell he’s anguished up there, and it’s a horrible thing to have to relive and talk about."
McLean said Patrick appeared to be compartmentalizing his emotions as he listened carefully to the questions and provided straightforward answers.
"He’s got to get through this," she said. "He’s got to listen to the questions and provide the answers as best he can, and I think that he’s doing that."
Lindsay Clancy reacts as the details of her children's deaths are read in court on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

Patrick testified that he was not concerned for the children’s safety when Lindsay first shared that the intrusive thoughts were telling her to hurt herself as well as her children. Moments after discussing the thoughts, he said, she could be seen making the children lunch, playing with them or preparing them for bed.

Patrick told jurors that he became alarmed after Lindsay was prescribed 13 psychiatric medications in the months prior to the murders and that he pushed for an in-person appointment because he believed there was a "disconnect" between the seriousness of her condition and the brief telehealth sessions she was receiving.
"It seemed like most of her telehealth appointments were pretty quick, and there just wasn’t, like, a lot of attention," he said.
Patrick also described taking Lindsay to hospital emergency departments and helping her enter McLean Hospital after she continued expressing suicidal thoughts.
He testified that he "would have paid anything" if insurance had become an obstacle to keeping her hospitalized.

Lindsay Clancy was indicted on three counts each of murder in the 2023 deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 7-month-old son Callan. She pleaded not guilty to the charges. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

The testimony could leave jurors asking whether the warning prompted an adequate response, McLean said, while cautioning against placing blame on Patrick or family members who may not have understood the severity of the risk.
"So many people don’t understand mental health today, so I’m not blaming him at all," McLean said. "Anybody might have done what he did, but that’s the part that scared me."
WATCH: Lindsay Clancy clutches tissues as jurors hear about her three children
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Patrick’s testimony followed starkly different opening statements from prosecutors and the defense.
Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham told jurors that Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were "deliberately and meticulously killed" by their mother on Jan. 24, 2023.

Buckingham alleged that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick from their Duxbury home to pick up medication and takeout food, giving herself enough time to strangle each child with an exercise band before attempting to kill herself.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

McLean said Buckingham gave jurors a "roadmap of cold, calculated intent" while humanizing each child's interests and focusing on the time and physical effort required to carry out three separate strangulations.

"The prosecution did that because she [Buckingham] wants the jury to remember that the act of strangulation takes time and physical effort," McLean said. "It requires a conscious choice to continue three separate times."
Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham delivers her opening statement in court on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
The Commonwealth’s strategy, she said, is to reject the defense’s bid that Clancy suffered a sudden psychotic break and instead portray her as organized, purposeful and controlled.
During opening statements, defense attorney Kevin Reddington conceded that Clancy killed the children but argued that the only meaningful dispute is what was happening inside her mind.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"She knows that she killed these children," Reddington told jurors. "The issue for consideration is what was going on in that woman’s mind."
McLean described the concession as a calculated move by a veteran trial attorney.
SEND US A TIP
"By doing that, he is attempting to strip the prosecution of their shock value and force the jury to look purely at Lindsay Clancy’s mental capacity," she said.
Reddington argued that Clancy had no motive to kill children she had loved and nurtured. He also displayed graphic hospital photographs showing Clancy with injuries to her neck and wrists.
GOT A TIP?
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is expected to last six to eight weeks, and the witness list contains more than 200 names. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)
McLean said the defense was framing Clancy’s paralysis "not as a consequence of a crime, but as the tragic final symptom of a complete postpartum psychotic break."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation. Her attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children but argue that she lacked criminal responsibility because of severe postpartum psychosis.
Judge William Sullivan told jurors that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when the children were killed.

"It’s going to be black and white for some people, gray area for other people," McLean said. "It is going to be one of the hardest things that this jury, or any jury, will ever have to decide."

title: California family members claim they were attacked at luxury Maui resort during violent melee
summary: A California family claims a group hurled chairs and beat relatives as young as 17 at the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina after racial threats.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A California family claims it was targeted in a racially motivated attack at a luxury Maui resort after a group allegedly hurled chairs and beat relatives ranging from teenagers to senior citizens during a chaotic poolside brawl.

Maui police confirmed to Fox News Digital that officers responded to the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina on July 17 around 10 p.m. for a disorderly incident involving approximately 30 people. Police said when officers arrived they found 10 to 15 people still gathered near the pool, several with visible injuries.

Police confirmed the preliminary investigation identified seven California victims between the ages of 17 and 62 who reported that a large group of juveniles assaulted multiple members of their party before fleeing.

According to Maui police, one victim told investigators he and his family were near the pool when an unknown male ran toward them asking for help. Moments later, several juvenile males allegedly chased the individual into the area before turning their attention to others nearby.
CITIES BRACE FOR HOLIDAY WEEKEND TEEN TAKEOVERS PUTTING BYSTANDERS AT DEADLY RISK, FORMER PROSECUTOR WARNS
An aerial view of the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina, Hawaii. (Kaanapali Alii Facebook)

"The group allegedly began throwing chairs and physically assaulting numerous people in the area, indiscriminately attacking individuals of all ages, including elderly family members who were struck during the incident," Maui police told Fox News Digital.
Family members told Hawaii News Now the alleged attackers repeatedly threatened to "beat up the haole boys" before the violence erupted.
Merriam-Webster defines "haole" as a Hawaiian term used to describe a foreigner or person of non-Hawaiian descent.
CRAZY BRAWL OVER A PARKING SPOT IN NEW YORK INCLUDES A VICIOUS SKATEBOARD TO THE HEAD
Low-angle view of the waters off Kaanapali Beach in Maui, Hawaii. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
The family told the outlet it wants the assault investigated as a hate crime. Maui police have not classified the incident as a hate crime.

One of the most seriously injured victims was a relative who was struck in the head with a chair while trying to protect family members, suffering a severe head wound that required 13 staples, according to the family.

Police told Fox News Digital that the investigation led to the arrest of a 20-year-old Makawao man on suspicion of second-degree assault. He was later released as the investigation continues. The case is currently classified as an assault/riot, and detectives have interviewed those involved while continuing to gather evidence.
SOCIALIST-LED CALIFORNIA CITY'S CLASH OVER ISRAEL AND ANTISEMITISM OFFERS GLIMPSE INTO THE LEFT'S FUTURE
A Maui Police Department vehicle in Lahaina, Hawaii. (Maui Police Department Facebook)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Kaanapali Alii said the safety and well-being of its guests, residents and team members "remains our highest priority" and that resort security responded immediately after the violence broke out.

"Upon learning of the altercation, our security team responded promptly, contacted the Maui Police Department and emergency medical services, and remained on scene to assist until first responders arrived," the resort said. "We have provided surveillance footage and are cooperating fully with law enforcement as their investigation continues."
The resort said it is also conducting its own internal review of the incident.

Addressing the family’s allegation that they were targeted because of their race, the resort said it takes claims of racial bias seriously but cautioned against drawing conclusions before detectives complete their investigation.

"We take allegations of this nature seriously," the statement said. "At this time, allegations regarding motive or the circumstances surrounding the incident have not been substantiated, and it would be inappropriate to speculate or draw conclusions while the investigation remains ongoing."

The resort also acknowledged that staff received reports of threats, harassment and disruptive behavior involving individuals connected to the incident before the violence erupted, but declined to discuss those complaints further because of the active criminal investigation.

Visitors walk along the Kaanapali Beachwalk amid palm trees and landscaped grounds overlooking Kaanapali North Beach at the Outrigger Honua Kai Resort and Spa, Lahaina, Maui, Hawaii, July 11, 2026. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

"Because this remains an active criminal investigation, we cannot comment on specific security actions, witness accounts or other details that could compromise the investigative process," the resort said.
The property said it remains committed to supporting investigators and those affected by the violence.
"Our focus remains on the well-being of our guests, residents and team members, and on assisting law enforcement in every way possible," the statement said.

title: Store clerk foiled ex-Navy SEAL's explosives plot targeting police at No Kings protest, feds say
summary: A store clerk's tip led federal agents to Gregory Vandenberg after he allegedly revealed his plan to hurl explosives at law enforcement during protests.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former U.S. Navy SEAL was convicted in a foiled plot to attack law enforcement officers with explosives during a "No Kings" protest in California after a store clerk's tip led federal investigators to him.

Gregory Vandenberg, 49, was found guilty after a five-day federal trial of transportation of explosives with intent to kill, injure or intimidate and attempted transportation of prohibited fireworks into California, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico.
Jurors deliberated for about three hours before returning the guilty verdict.

Prosecutors said Vandenberg was driving from El Paso, Texas, to San Diego ahead of the June 14, 2025, demonstrations when he stopped at a travel center near Lordsburg, New Mexico, and purchased six mortar-style fireworks and 72 M-150 firecrackers.
FORMER MARINE GETS 100 YEARS IN PRISON AS JUDGE CALLS ICE DETENTION CENTER AMBUSH 'AN ASSAULT ON DEMOCRACY'

Surveillance video shows Gregory Vandenberg speaking with a store employee while purchasing fireworks in New Mexico. Employees later contacted law enforcement after he discussed attacking officers at California's No Kings protests, federal authorities said. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)
While making the purchase, Vandenberg told a store clerk he intended to throw the explosives at law enforcement officers during the protests, federal authorities said.

He repeatedly asked about the amount of gunpowder in the fireworks, whether taping multiple mortars together would increase their explosive force and said he was interested only in their ability to injure officers, prosecutors said.
'SOMETHING BIG': FEDS REVEAL HOW RELATIVES OF SUSPECTS IN FOILED WHITE HOUSE UFC PLOT SAW WARNING SIGNS
Gregory Vandenberg wears a shirt reading "AMALEK" while purchasing fireworks at a New Mexico travel center on June 12, 2025. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

Vandenberg also encouraged the clerk to attend the protests and hand out fireworks to others, telling the employee he would not get hurt because of his military experience, according to trial testimony.
The conversation alarmed employees enough that they wrote down Vandenberg's license plate and contacted law enforcement before he reached California.
Federal agents tracked Vandenberg to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Tucson, Arizona, where he was arrested the following morning while sleeping inside his vehicle.
ANTI-ISRAEL DEMONSTRATOR SENTENCED TO YEAR IN JAIL FOR MANSLAUGHTER DURING 2023 PROTESTS
Prosecutors said he falsely claimed he was traveling for work despite being unemployed and later told investigators he was visiting friends in Phoenix.
A search of Vandenberg's vehicle uncovered the fireworks along with clothing displaying antisemitic, anti-Israel and extremist imagery, according to prosecutors.

Among the items recovered were shirts bearing an Al-Qaeda flag, a shirt calling for the destruction of Judea, a hat featuring the Al-Qaeda flag and apparel displaying a variation of the Black Sun, a symbol associated with neo-Nazi ideology.

Federal prosecutors said investigators recovered an Al-Qaeda flag hat from Gregory Vandenberg's vehicle after his arrest en route to California's No Kings protests. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

Jurors were also shown photographs of Vandenberg wearing a custom-made T-shirt bearing the word "AMALEK" while inside the travel center. Prosecutors said Vandenberg told investigators the word meant "destroyer of Jews."

Investigators also discovered Vandenberg's cellphone home screen displayed a Taliban flag. A forensic review of the phone uncovered what prosecutors described as violent extremist content, including antisemitic, anti-Israel and anti-U.S. material, as well as messages discussing the upcoming protests.

Federal investigators recovered clothing bearing extremist and antisemitic imagery from Gregory Vandenberg's vehicle, according to court records. (United States Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico)

According to prosecutors, those messages suggested Vandenberg believed the U.S. government, including President Donald Trump, was controlled by Israel and Jewish people, evidence they argued helped establish his motive for targeting law enforcement officers.

"People in this country are free to hold their own beliefs and to express them peacefully," Acting U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison said in a statement. "What they are not free to do is use explosives to threaten or terrorize others."

Ellison added that Vandenberg "intended to turn explosives into a tool of intimidation," and said the verdict "sends the message that attempts to substitute violence for expressing one's opinion has no place in our communities and will be met with federal consequences."
Vandenberg was later sentenced to 16 months in federal prison, where he remains in custody. Upon his release, he will serve one year of supervised release.

title: Woman wins massive settlement after bladder mistakenly removed during surgery for benign cyst
summary: A Maine jury awarded a woman $17 million after a routine surgery for a benign ovarian cyst ended with the accidental removal of her bladder.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Maine woman has been awarded $17 million after a catastrophic surgical error resulted in the removal of her bladder during a procedure intended to address a benign ovarian cyst.

The damages were awarded to Emily Mitchell last Thursday by a Kennebec County jury following a two-week medical malpractice trial against Northern Light Inland Hospital and Northern Light Health, according to her attorneys on Friday. The verdict is reportedly the largest medical malpractice award in Kennebec County.
The devastating procedure occurred on March 1, 2023, and resulted in what Mitchell’s attorneys described as an irreversible injury with extreme health repercussions that are still ongoing.
"According to evidence presented at trial, what began as a routine gynecologic surgery resulted in one of the most devastating surgical errors imaginable," Berman & Simmons said in a statement.
FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL
Northern Light Inland Hospital in Waterville closed in May 2025. (Google Maps)
Northern Light Inland Hospital in Waterville officially closed in May 2025 after serving the community for more than 80 years, according to the state.

The healthcare system cited "immense pressure of higher operational costs, unsustainably low reimbursement rates, and a tight labor market" as factors behind the closure in a statement issued that month.
According to the attorneys, Michell scheduled the surgery after imaging showed that a benign ovarian cyst had significantly increased in size.
'I THOUGHT I HAD THE FLU': MOM NEARLY DIED AFTER DISMISSING DEADLY SEPSIS SYMPTOMS
FILE - Emily Mitchell won a record medical malpractice verdict after a devastating surgical mistake left her permanently dependent on ongoing treatment. (iStock)
Following the procedure, Mitchell’s condition worsened, and she was transferred to another hospital for emergency surgery.

Surgeons later discovered that her bladder had been removed during the original operation, and pathology confirmed the tissue taken during the procedure was "full-thickness bladder tissue," according to her attorneys.
The damage appeared irreversible, as "surgeons determined there was insufficient healthy bladder tissue remaining to reconstruct or repair the organ," according to Berman & Simmons.

For the next eight months, Mitchell relied on bilateral nephrostomy tubes to drain urine directly from her kidneys. The treatment involves thin plastic tubes surgically placed through the skin of the lower back and into both kidneys, allowing urine to flow into external bags attached to the exposed ends of the tubes.
During that time, Mitchell reportedly experienced recurring urinary tract infections, kidney infections, multiple medical procedures and ongoing complications.
OHIO APPROVES NEARLY BILLION-DOLLAR PAYMENT AFTER COURT RULED STATE SHORTCHANGED NURSING HOMES
FILE - A routine gynecologic procedure turned life-altering after surgeons mistakenly removed a Maine woman's bladder, leading to a $17 million jury award. (iStock)
She was eventually referred to Massachusetts for complex reconstructive surgery, where surgeons used a portion of her small intestine to create a new bladder, known as a neobladder.
Mitchell’s attorneys said she "continues to live with the permanent effects of those injuries" nearly three years after the original operation.
She must insert a catheter multiple times a day to drain the neobladder and requires ongoing medical treatment from specialists related to the loss of her bladder.

After hearing the evidence, the jury found Northern Light Inland Hospital and Northern Light Health liable and awarded Mitchell damages covering past and future medical expenses, suffering, loss of enjoyment of life, emotional distress and permanent impairment.

"For our clients, this isn't just a legal victory—it's the closure they've needed for a long time," attorney Susan A. Faunce said in a statement.

"They can finally begin to move forward, knowing that what happened to them was seen, heard, and acknowledged. This verdict won't undo the pain our clients have endured, but it does offer something they haven't had in a long time: closure. They can finally put this chapter behind them."

title: Luigi Mangione plea talks raise showdown over Brian Thompson murder trial
summary: Manhattan prosecutors warn they could oppose any federal plea deal for Luigi Mangione that may interfere with his New York murder trial set for Sept. 8.
story: Accused CEO killer Luigi Mangione's defense criticizes reports of a possible plea deal with federal prosecutors. His attorneys claim this information is part of a deliberate pattern to manipulate public opinion and violate his fair trial rights. The defense also withdrew an emotional distress claim in Mangione's state murder case, which could have reduced his murder charge to manslaughter.

Manhattan prosecutors are signaling they could fight a federal plea deal for Luigi Mangione if it threatens to derail his upcoming New York murder trial in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

In a newly unsealed letter reviewed by Fox News Digital, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office said it is aware of reports that Mangione could seek a guilty plea in his separate federal case before the state trial begins.
Prosecutors warned that if such a deal would interfere with New York's prosecution, they could ask the federal judge to take that into account before accepting it.

The filing follows a June hearing in federal court, where U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett pushed Mangione's federal trial to January 2027, clearing the way for his New York murder trial to move forward first.
LUIGI MANGIONE'S FEDERAL TRIAL PUSHED TO NEXT YEAR IN ASSASSINATION OF UNITEDHEALTHCARE CEO
Luigi Mangione appears at an evidence suppression hearing at the Manhattan Supreme Court in New York City, May 18, 2026. (Steven Hirsch/New York Post via Pool)

Mangione, 28, has pleaded not guilty in both the state and federal cases stemming from the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, who was shot outside a Manhattan hotel as he headed to a conference.

"If a proposed federal guilty plea would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution, the People could advise the federal district court of that consequence, and the court should consider that fact in deciding whether to accept the plea," Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann wrote in the July 2 letter.
LUIGI MANGIONE'S EMOTIONAL DISTURBANCE DEFENSE MAY HAVE HUGE IMPACT IN HIS OTHER CASE: LAWYER
Prosecutors added that the court should also consider any opposition from Thompson's family before accepting such a plea.
The letter marks the clearest sign yet that Manhattan prosecutors are prepared to push back against any deal they believe could keep the state's high-profile murder case from ever reaching a jury.
The DA's office said it has already shared its position with federal prosecutors and Mangione's defense team.
LUIGI MANGIONE OVERRULED HIS OWN LAWYERS WITH A 'CHANGE OF HEART' ON PSYCH DEFENSE, LEGAL EXPERT SAYS
Luigi Mangione in Court at 100 Centre Street in Manhattan for a pretrial evidence hearing, Thursday, December 11th, 2025. (William Farrington for New York Post via Pool)

Prosecutors argued that any resolution should reflect "the seriousness of defendant's offenses," "the loss of an innocent life," the impact on Thompson's family and New York's interest in prosecuting the homicide.
The dispute comes after reports surfaced in June that Mangione's legal team and federal prosecutors had discussed a possible plea deal but failed to reach an agreement.
Mangione attorney Karen Friedman Agnifilo blasted information attributed to anonymous sources at the time as "a troubling, deliberate pattern by prosecutors and law enforcement to prejudice Luigi."
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York previously declined to comment on the reported negotiations.
At a June 29 hearing, Garnett delayed Mangione's federal trial after concluding there was no practical way for his attorneys to prepare for two high-profile trials at the same time.
During that hearing, Agnifilo confirmed Mangione's New York murder trial remained on track to begin Sept. 8 and said the defense had been told there would be no delays.
"We've been told that no requests for adjournments will be granted and to be ready on that date," Agnifilo told the court.
The judge said there was simply no realistic way to move both cases forward at once.

"It's simply impossible for us to be moving through the jury selection process in this case while the defendant and his counsel are fully occupied actually conducting the state trial," the judge said. She rescheduled federal jury selection for Jan. 5, 2027, with opening statements set for Jan. 25.
Luigi Mangione appears at an evidence suppression hearing at the Manhattan Supreme Court in New York City, May 18, 2026. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters via Pool)
Under the revised schedule, about 800 prospective jurors will complete written questionnaires in early December before in-person jury selection begins.

Manhattan prosecutors also argued New York should get the first opportunity to try Mangione because he was extradited there on the state case before he was later transferred into federal custody. Prosecutors argued that the transfer did not change New York's priority to prosecute him first.

Prosecutors allege Mangione fled the city and was arrested five days later at a McDonald's in Altoona, Pennsylvania.
Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz contributed to this report.

title: Illegal immigrant accused of murdering college student dials into hearing from hospital bed
summary: Jose Medina appeared via Zoom from a hospital bed after a reported seizure as prosecutors revealed new DNA testing evidence in the Sheridan Gorman case.
story: Retired NYPD inspector and attorney Paul Mauro critiques the health defense of Jose Medina, the alleged killer of Loyola University student Sheridan Gorman, on 'The Story.'

The illegal immigrant accused of gunning down 18-year-old Loyola University freshman Sheridan Gorman appeared in court Monday from a hospital bed after suffering a reported seizure, according to his defense attorney.

Jose Medina-Medina, a Venezuelan national charged with Gorman's murder, did not appear in person for a hearing before a Cook County judge. Instead, he joined the proceedings remotely via Zoom from a local hospital, where his attorney said he was admitted after experiencing a seizure over the weekend.
The judge ordered Medina to appear in person at his next court hearing if he is physically able.
Defense attorneys have repeatedly argued that Medina has suffered seizures and other health issues stemming from a 2018 shooting in Colombia, where they say he was shot in the head.
TEENS SUSPECTED OF MURDERING CONGRESSIONAL INTERN LINKED BY DNA ON SHELL CASINGS, PROSECUTORS SAY
Jose Medina-Medina shows his head injury in a jail picture. (Cook County Sheriff's Office)
On Monday, Medina's attorney told the judge the defense is still waiting for additional information about his medical condition before deciding which pretrial motions it may file.
Meanwhile, prosecutors said the murder case continues to progress.

They told the court they have turned over several additional pieces of evidence to the defense, including most of the DNA testing completed on the firearm recovered at the scene. Trace evidence testing is still underway, and prosecutors said they may request additional DNA analysis depending on those results.
GIANNO CALDWELL: FOUR YEARS AFTER MY BROTHER’S MURDER, I’M MARCHING FOR JUSTICE
Loyola University Chicago student Sheridan Gorman poses with the school’s mascot during a campus event in an undated photo. (Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

Prosecutors also said they've turned over more evidence in the separate case accusing Medina of possessing a homemade shank while in custody. They are still waiting for subpoenaed body-camera video and hospital surveillance video to be added to the case.
The case was continued until Sept. 3 for another status hearing.
Sheridan Gorman's family did not attend Monday's hearing.
Madelon, Jess and Tom Gorman, family members of Sheridan Gorman, appeared on "The Story" to discuss the death of their daughter and sister. ("The Story"/Fox News)

title: Savannah Guthrie delivers 'very specific' message to mom's kidnapper 25 weeks after her abduction
summary: Savannah Guthrie posted an emotional Instagram plea with a "very specific" message directed at whoever kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie.
story: Savannah Guthrie issued a new plea on Instagram to those who kidnapped her mother, Nancy Guthrie, in a video posted July 27, 2026. (Credit: @savannahguthrie/Instagram)
Savannah Guthrie delivered a "very specific" message to her mother's kidnapper on Monday, more than 25 weeks after the 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie vanished from her Arizona home.

In an emotional plea posted to her Instagram account, Savannah Guthrie appealed directly to whoever is responsible for the kidnapping, saying that her family is "in agony" and "will never stop looking for her."
"Do the right thing now," Guthrie urged her mother's unidentified kidnappers. "Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her."
NANCY GUTHRIE UPDATE: 25 WEEKS AFTER ABDUCTION, ELIZABETH SMART SAYS THERE'S ‘REASON TO HAVE HOPE’
An undated photo of Nancy Guthrie and Savannah Guthrie, provided by NBC in response to the disappearance of the 84-year-old mother of the 'Today' host. (Courtesy of NBC)

"I'm coming on today with a very specific message. It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts. The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place," Savannah Guthrie said. "I truly believe it is never too late to do right thing. Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us. No matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."

A federal source close to the Guthrie case told Fox News that Savannah Guthrie was in communication with law enforcement about releasing her newest video. It was her first message in weeks, as official updates have slowed to a trickle and there have been no signs of her mother's whereabouts.
NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF ‘TODAY’ HOST'S MOM

Savannah Guthrie and her husband, Michael Feldman, were seen arriving at LaGuardia Airport in New York City on the morning of July 17 as the couple prepared to head out of town. Guthrie had just wrapped up hosting her portion of the "Today" broadcast and had walked off the set a day earlier, when an intruder breached security and accosted colleague Craig Melvin. She has been off-air since filming a new "Wordle" game show. (T. Jackson/Backgrid)
The family is asking anyone with information to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI and claim a reward of over $1 million.

The elder Guthrie, 84, was taken from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood in the early hours of Feb. 1, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department.

The results of DNA testing and other forensics have not been made public as the case drags on without signs of Guthrie. A purported ransom note and an apparent follow-up message that claimed she had died have not been confirmed as authentic by investigators.
No suspects have been publicly identified.

Earlier in the case, two men were detained, questioned and released without charges after searches of their vehicles and family homes. Neither has been accused of wrongdoing in connection with Guthrie's disappearance.

Emergency personnel responded around 9:30 a.m. Wednesday after reports of an unresponsive person floating in shallow water, the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office said. Bryn Waite was pronounced dead at the scene.

title: Bryan Kohberger waived his appeal rights but plans on pursuing post-conviction relief
summary: Bryan Kohberger plans to file for post-conviction relief after pleading guilty to killing four University of Idaho students, two sources say.
story: The longtime attorney and true crime host says prosecutors had a "slam dunk" case against Bryan Kohberger, which led to the plea deal — dismissing his defense claims of shaky evidence against the convicted killer.

The admitted murderer Bryan Kohberger plans to file for post-conviction relief after pleading guilty to killing four University of Idaho students in a 4 a.m. home invasion attack, according to court records.
Kohberger plans to argue that he had bad counsel. Court records show he filed a petition for post-conviction relief Monday.

Kohberger, in his handwritten petition, claims that he was "convinced to falsely confess," claiming his high-profile defense team of Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow didn't tell him about "exculpatory discovery" — evidence mentioned in the recent "Broken Plea" book but never vetted in court.
Read the filing here:

The New York Times was first to report this story after Kohberger called a reporter directly and claimed that he has an "absolute claim of innocence" in his first public remarks outside the courtroom.
IDAHO MURDERS EVIDENCE LEAK TRIGGERS CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION FOR INSIDER WHO SPILLED SECRETS: REPORT

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse in Boise, Idaho, on July 23, 2025, for sentencing in the University of Idaho murders case, where prosecutors relied heavily on cellphone location data and digital evidence. (Photo by Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)
"My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn," he told the outlet.

The family of victim Kaylee Goncalves ripped into Kohberger and his supporters as "the mosquito you just can't seem to swat." Kohberger's petition fails to acknowledge that he told Idaho Judge Steven Hippler last year that he "knowingly, voluntarily and intelligently" admitted to the crime in court, the family said in a statement.

"Quite the opposite," the statement continued. "He appeared in court for a hearing before a judge, accompanied by his four lawyers. He chose not to leave his fate—or the facts of the case—to a jury. He never cried foul, never claimed he was uninformed or pressured, and never suggested there were problems with the discovery materials he and his counsel had reviewed for two years that should have been challenged. He admitted his guilt. When asked whether he was actually guilty, he answered, 'Yes.'"
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
The family would have preferred the case go to trial with the death penalty still on the table.
"Instead, BK received exactly what he asked for: a deal that spared his life," the family said. "Know this—he hates that life."
Kohberger has repeatedly complained about prison conditions as he sits in isolation at the Idaho Maximum Security Institute.
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador told Fox News Digital his office is "ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."
"My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news," he said.

Madison Mogen, top left, smiles on the shoulders of her best friend, Kaylee Goncalves, as they pose with Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and two other housemates in Goncalves' final Instagram post, shared the day before the four students were stabbed to death. (@kayleegoncalves/Instagram)

Labrador's office assisted Latah County prosecutors in defeating virtually all of Kohberger's pretrial motions seeking to suppress evidence in the case, which resulted in his guilty plea weeks before he would have gone to trial and faced the potential death penalty if convicted.
In his message to the Times, Kohberger claimed that "justice was not served" and that it was "circumnavigated by a broken plea."

"Broken Plea" is the title of a recent book about the case that shed new light on what the defense may have looked like at trial — and his use of the term surprised author Chris Whitcomb, who says he had never spoken to Kohberger.
"He would have to show ‘manifest injustice,’" said Joshua Ritter, a California-based defense attorney and Fox News contributor. "Essentially his lawyers lied to him."
A watchman parked outside 1122 King Road on Dec. 11, 2022, four weeks after four students were stabbed to death inside. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)
One hypothesis floated in Whitcomb's book is that Kohberger may not have fully understood or meaningfully participated in the decision to plead guilty.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Kohberger is serving four consecutive life sentences with no possibility of parole plus another 10 years for the Nov. 13, 2022 murders of Xana Kernodle, Ethan Chapin, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves after pleading guilty in July 2025.

Police found his DNA on a knife sheath in a bed with two of the four victims, Mogen and Goncalves. They also tracked his vehicle coming and going, and forensic investigators were prepared to testify about how, although he shut his phone off during the murders, the evidence suggested he drove to and from the crime scene anyway.

As part of the plea deal, he waived his right to an appeal — and Monday's filing caught some of the victims' relatives by surprise.
"I didn't think he could do that, since that was part of the stipulation in the first place — he wasn't going to be able to do that," said Cara Northington, Kernodle's mother.

title: Japan mall rebuilt after deadly 2016 earthquake destroyed in major temblor weeks after 'fresh start' reopening
summary: A massive explosion ripped through Aeon Mall in Kumamoto just weeks after its grand reopening, leaving up to 30 employees unaccounted for.
story: Video from a surveillance camera shows stationary trucks shaking after an earthquake hit Kumamoto, Japan. (Credit: Reuters)

A shopping mall in southern Japan that had just reopened after years of reconstruction following a devastating 2016 earthquake was destroyed Tuesday after a powerful earthquake struck the region and was followed by a massive explosion, leaving dozens of workers unaccounted for.
The Aeon Mall in Kumamoto Prefecture celebrated its grand reopening on June 13 after years of rebuilding meant to mark the region's recovery from the 2016 disaster.

Just weeks later, a magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck near Kumamoto, according to FOX Weather, citing the U.S. Geological Survey. Japan's Meteorological Agency measured the same quake at magnitude 7.1 using its own seismic scale.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS

An aerial view shows a collapsed chimney at Nippon Paper Industries' Yatsushiro Mill after an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, in Yatsushiro, July 28, 2026. (yodo/via Reuters/TPX Images of the Day)

About 200 shoppers were safely evacuated after the earthquake, officials said. Roughly an hour later, a powerful explosion ripped through the building, blowing off exterior walls and exposing its steel framework. NHK reported that about 20 to 30 mall employees remained unaccounted for, while police said rescuers could not immediately enter because of the risk of aftershocks.

The mall had become one of the most visible symbols of Kumamoto's recovery after the magnitude 7.3 earthquake that devastated the region in April 2016. Aeon said the redevelopment included seismic reinforcements and other safety improvements designed to make the complex more resilient.

Witnesses reported smelling gas before the explosion, according to Reuters. An Aeon spokesperson said employees immediately helped evacuate visitors after the quake, while prefectural officials confirmed about 200 people were guided safely outside before the blast.
EXCLUSIVE: FRANKLIN GRAHAM VISITS EMERGENCY HOSPITAL TREATING VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS

The damaged Aeon Mall shopping centre, where, according to local media, an explosion occurred after an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan's southern Kumamoto Prefecture, in Kashima Town, July 28, 2026.  (Kyodo/via Reuters)

According to FOX Weather, the earthquake struck just before 4:30 p.m. local time about 9 miles north of Kumamoto at a depth of roughly 6 miles. Japan's Meteorological Agency briefly issued and later lifted a tsunami advisory for parts of Kyushu. NHK reported at least 50 people were injured, while Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency said the quake sparked at least eight fires. Kumamoto Airport also temporarily closed.
Reuters reported the mall welcomed more than 8 million visitors annually after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. opened a factory nearby in 2024.

The complex housed about 200 stores, a movie theater and parking for roughly 5,000 vehicles. It also became known locally after a supermarket inside sold 10-yen onigiri to help survivors following the 2016 earthquake.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rescue workers conduct a search and rescue operation at the damaged Aeon Mall in Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, in Kashima Town, July 28, 2026. (Credit: Japan Out via Reuters)
When the mall reopened in June, Aeon described the project as a "'re-start' initiative" marking both the shopping center's 21st anniversary and the region's recovery from the 2016 earthquake.
As night fell Tuesday, rescue operations remained on hold because of continuing aftershocks as families awaited word on the employees still believed to be inside.
